definition: The earthy, pleasant scent produced when rain falls on dry soil after a warm, dry spell.
exampleSentence: The first fat drops hit the parched garden and that smell rose up - petrichor, the whole street suddenly breathing again.
etymology: Coined by CSIRO scientists Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas in 'Nature of Argillaceous Odour' (Nature, 7 March 1964) as an 'ichor' or 'tenuous essence derived from rock or stone,' from Greek 'petra' (stone) + 'ichor' (the fluid in the veins of the gods).

definition: The occurrence of happy or beneficial discoveries by accident, plus the wit to notice them.
exampleSentence: She went to the library for a tax form and left with the novel that changed her life - pure serendipity.
etymology: Coined by Horace Walpole in a letter to Horace Mann dated 28 January 1754 - 'a very expressive word' - from the Persian tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' whose heroes kept making lucky discoveries.

definition: The warmth of the sun in winter.
exampleSentence: She dragged the kitchen chair onto the icy balcony just to sit in the apricity for ten borrowed minutes.
etymology: From Latin 'apricitas' (warmed by the sun); first recorded in Henry Cockeram's 'English Dictionarie' (1623) as 'the warmenes of the Sunne in winter,' and now obsolete - the same root gave us 'apricot.'

definition: Twilight; the dusk of the evening.
exampleSentence: In the gloaming the hills went violet and the first window lights came on one by one.
etymology: From Old English 'glōmung,' related to 'glōm' (twilight) and to 'glow' - the soft glow that lingers after sunset.

definition: Denoting a past period of idyllic peace and happiness.
exampleSentence: They talked all night about the halcyon summers before everyone scattered across the map.
etymology: From Greek 'halkyon' (kingfisher), a bird the ancients believed calmed the sea while nesting on it at the winter solstice - the 'halcyon days.'

definition: The vault of the sky; the heavens or upper air.
exampleSentence: Their cheers rose until the very welkin seemed to ring.
etymology: From Old English wolcen 'cloud'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The armpit; chiefly in Scottish and Irish usage.
exampleSentence: He tucked the newspaper under his oxter and hurried off.
etymology: Alteration of Old English oxta, akin to eax 'axis, axle'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A song or poem greeting the dawn, or about lovers parting at daybreak.
exampleSentence: He wrote her an aubade to be sung as the sky paled.
etymology: From French, 'dawn serenade', from Old Occitan auba 'dawn'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To move forward with an ungainly, bounding, lolling motion.
exampleSentence: The big dog lolloped across the field to greet us.
etymology: Probably from 'loll' plus a frequentative ending; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A cloud formation of pouch-like lobes hanging from the underside of a larger cloud.
exampleSentence: Eerie mammatus drooped beneath the thunderhead before the storm.
etymology: From Latin mamma 'breast, udder'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Joy felt at a loved one's happiness in another relationship.
exampleSentence: Watching her partner laugh with his girlfriend, she felt genuine compersion, not jealousy.
etymology: Coined on 28 November 1980 by the Kerista Commune via an alphabet board; a headword in Dictionary.com, which dates first use to 1990-95.

definition: The joyful anticipation that comes from imagining a future pleasure.
exampleSentence: Booking the trip filled her with months of delicious vorfreude.
etymology: German 'vor' (before) + 'Freude' (joy); a documented loanword explored in The Guardian's 9 April 2024 feature on anticipatory joy.

definition: The overwhelming urge to squeeze something unbearably cute.
exampleSentence: Seeing the puppy's fat little paws, she was seized by gigil.
etymology: From Tagalog 'gigil'; added to the Oxford English Dictionary in its March 2025 update, with English usage dated to 1990.

definition: The Swedish principle of 'just the right amount'; balanced moderation.
exampleSentence: Their home embodied lagom: enough comfort, nothing excessive.
etymology: Swedish 'lagom' (just right); a headword in Dictionary.com.

definition: One's friends and acquaintances, as distinct from kin.
exampleSentence: He returned to the village to be among his kith and kin once more.
etymology: From Old English 'cyththu' (kinsfolk), from 'cunnan' (to know); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The soft sound of wind whispering through trees.
exampleSentence: They stopped talking just to hear the psithurism move across the poplars.
etymology: From Greek psithuros 'whispering, slanderous' — onomatopoeic, the word breathes like the sound.

definition: The low, distant rumble of thunder.
exampleSentence: All afternoon a brontide rolled along the horizon, but the rain never came.
etymology: From Greek brontē 'thunder'.

definition: A love of night and darkness; finding peace after dark.
exampleSentence: Her nyctophilia kept her up till three, happiest when the house went quiet and black.
etymology: From Greek nyx 'night' + philia 'love'.

definition: Of or occurring in the evening.
exampleSentence: The garden kept vespertine hours — its white flowers opened only at dusk.
etymology: From Latin vesper 'evening'.

definition: The beauty found in imperfection, impermanence, and the worn.
exampleSentence: The cracked, mended bowl was lovelier for the flaw — pure wabi-sabi.
etymology: Japanese wabi 'rustic simplicity' + sabi 'the beauty of age and wear'.

definition: The gap at the base of a hedge made by the regular passage of a small animal.
exampleSentence: A tuft of fur on the bramble showed where a fox slipped nightly through the smeuse.
etymology: Sussex dialect noun, popularised by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks' (2015); related to dialect 'smeuse/smout', to creep through a gap.

definition: The thin film of ice that lacquers leaves, twigs and grass when a freeze follows a partial thaw, making a whole landscape glitter in sunlight.
exampleSentence: Dawn lit the ammil and the hedgerow seemed strung with glass.
etymology: Devon dialect, thought to descend from Old English 'ammel', meaning enamel; recorded by Robert Macfarlane in 'Landmarks'.

definition: The habit of acquiring books and letting them pile up unread.
exampleSentence: His nightstand was a monument to tsundoku, six novels deep and none of them opened.
etymology: Japanese, a Meiji-era pun blending 'tsunde-oku' (to pile up and leave) with 'dokusho' (reading books); the 'oku' was swapped for 'doku' (to read).

definition: The leisurely conversation that lingers at the table after a meal is finished but before anyone gets up.
exampleSentence: Lunch ended at two, but the sobremesa carried us, laughing, well past five.
etymology: Spanish, literally 'over the table', from 'sobre' (over) + 'mesa' (table).

definition: A beer enjoyed outdoors, especially the first one savoured in the open air on a fine day.
exampleSentence: The instant the sun broke through, the whole café spilled onto the pavement for a utepils.
etymology: Norwegian, from 'ute' (outside) + 'pils' (pilsner/lager); added to the Oxford English Dictionary as a loanword filling a lexical gap.

definition: The rumbling, gurgling sound made by gas moving through the intestines.
exampleSentence: In the silent exam hall, his borborygmus was practically a public announcement.
etymology: New Latin, from Greek 'borborygmos', from 'borboryzein' (to rumble) — itself an imitation of the gut's noise.

definition: A queasy, fluttering stomach brought on by nerves; butterflies with an upset edge.
exampleSentence: I had the collywobbles all morning before walking out to give my speech.
etymology: English, dating to around 1823; a 'fanciful formation' (OED) probably reshaping New Latin 'cholera morbus' under the influence of 'colic' and 'wobble'.

definition: A shrewd, utterly unprincipled person, especially a politician who chases office with no regard for party or principle.
exampleSentence: Every election season the airwaves fill with snollygosters promising everything to everyone.
etymology: American English, first known use 1845; probably an alteration of 'snallygaster', a mythical poultry-preying creature of rural Maryland (though that word is attested later, so the link is uncertain).

definition: A habitually smiling face, or the relentlessly cheerful person wearing it.
exampleSentence: Before coffee I can't bear a gigglemug grinning at me across the breakfast table.
etymology: Victorian English slang, recorded in 19th-century dictionaries of slang, combining 'giggle' with 'mug' in its slang sense of 'face'.

definition: Fresh hope; a recovery from despair.
exampleSentence: The first warm morning after a long illness filled her with sudden respair.
etymology: English, with a single Oxford English Dictionary record dated to 1525; the positive counterpart of 'despair', from Latin 'sperare' (to hope).

definition: The restless anticipation of a guest's arrival that keeps sending you to the window or door to check.
exampleSentence: Full of iktsuarpok, she checked the street a dozen times before his car finally turned in.
etymology: From Inuktitut (an Inuit language of the Canadian Arctic), describing the impatient excitement of waiting for someone to come.

definition: The bracing shock felt when first plunging into cold water.
exampleSentence: The curglaff of the loch knocked the breath clean out of me before the swim turned blissful.
etymology: Scots dialect, from 'cur-' (a prefix marking something going awry) + 'glaff' (a sudden blast); recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language.

definition: The shimmering, road-like reflection the moon casts across water.
exampleSentence: A silver mångata stretched from the shore to the horizon, as if you could walk to the moon.
etymology: Swedish, from 'måne' (moon) + 'gata' (street, road) — literally 'moon-street'.

definition: Shimmering with a band of shifting lustre, like a cat's eye or polished tiger's-eye stone.
exampleSentence: The silk shifted from green to gold as she moved, chatoyant in the candlelight.
etymology: French, present participle of 'chatoyer' (to shine like a cat's eyes), from 'chat' (cat).

definition: Glowing or flickering softly, with a gentle radiance that plays over a surface without burning.
exampleSentence: Lambent firelight moved across the ceiling as the logs settled.
etymology: From Latin 'lambens', present participle of 'lambere' (to lick); first used in English in the 17th century of flame appearing to 'lick' a surface.

definition: Of grey skies, fog and short sunless days; wintry and misty.
exampleSentence: November settled in, brumous and dim, and the lamps came on by four.
etymology: From French 'brume' (mist, fog), via Latin 'bruma' (winter, the shortest day).

definition: Feeling sick and seedy from too much eating or drinking; hungover.
exampleSentence: He shuffled crapulent into the kitchen, vowing never to mix wines again.
etymology: From Late Latin 'crapulentus', from Latin 'crapula' (intoxication, the after-effects of drink), itself from Greek 'kraipale'.

definition: Pleasantly round and cuddly in build.
exampleSentence: A jolly-timbered uncle in a too-tight waistcoat carved the goose with great ceremony.
etymology: 18th-century English; 'timbered' in the old sense of 'built, framed' (as of a body's frame) softened by 'jolly'.

definition: To gaze longingly and silently at someone who is eating, in the hope of being offered some.
exampleSentence: The dog sat groking at my sandwich with such soulful eyes that I caved.
etymology: Scots dialect (also 'growk'), recorded in the Scottish National Dictionary; of uncertain origin, used of children and dogs begging at the table.

definition: To dash about frantically tidying the house in the short window between learning a guest is coming and their knock at the door.
exampleSentence: Her text gave me ten minutes to scurryfunge before she rang the bell.
etymology: English dialect; from 'scurry' (to rush) with an obscure second element, its sense shifting from 'to scour/scrub' to a hasty tidy-up by the mid-19th century. Still heard in Newfoundland dialect.

definition: To laugh loudly, hard and uncontrollably.
exampleSentence: The whole table began to cachinnate until people at the next booth turned to stare.
etymology: From Latin 'cachinnare' (to laugh aloud), an imitative word echoing the sound of raucous laughter.

definition: To leave abruptly and without ceremony; to make off.
exampleSentence: The moment the bill arrived, he absquatulated to the bathroom and never returned.
etymology: A jocular 19th-century American coinage built on mock-Latin lines, riffing on 'squat' to suggest the opposite of settling down.

definition: To hesitate awkwardly while introducing someone because you've forgotten their name.
exampleSentence: I began to tartle at the party, buying time with 'Of course you two know each other!'
etymology: Scots, recorded in dictionaries of the Scots language; an expressive word for the social stumble of a forgotten name.

definition: The instinctive full-body stretch, often paired with a yawn, that you perform on waking.
exampleSentence: She rose with a luxurious pandiculation, arms flung wide and jaw cracking in a yawn.
etymology: From Latin 'pandiculari' (to stretch oneself), from 'pandere' (to spread, stretch); in English from the 1610s–1640s, first recorded by lexicographer Randle Cotgrave in 1611.

definition: The curved web of space between the outstretched thumb and forefinger.
exampleSentence: He balanced the pencil in the purlicue of his hand while he thought.
etymology: Scots, first recorded 1808 in John Jamieson's dictionary; probably from Scots 'pirlie' (curly, twisted), perhaps via 'pirl' (to twist or spin).

definition: A cold sea-fog that rolls in off the North Sea onto the east coast of Scotland and northern England.
exampleSentence: By noon the haar had swallowed the harbour, and the foghorns began their mournful lowing.
etymology: Scots and northern English, recorded from the 17th–18th centuries; probably from Middle Dutch/Low German 'hare' (a biting cold wind), with some influence from Old Norse 'hárr' (hoary, grey).

definition: A person who idly watches activity on a canal — or, more broadly, anyone who stares at length at anything.
exampleSentence: A row of gongoozlers leaned on the lock gates, happily watching the narrowboats rise.
etymology: Canal-workers' slang, first recorded 1904 in H. R. de Salis's 'Bradshaw's Canals', defined as 'an idle and inquisitive person who stands staring'; perhaps from Lincolnshire dialect 'gawn' and 'gooze', both meaning to stare or gape.

definition: A lover of travel and the open road.
exampleSentence: An incurable hodophile, she kept a packed bag by the door year-round.
etymology: From Greek 'hodos' (road, journey) + '-phile' (lover); part of a small family with 'hodophilia' and its antonym 'hodophobia'.

definition: Studied carelessness; the art of making something difficult look entirely effortless.
exampleSentence: He wore the tuxedo with such sprezzatura — tie loosened, collar undone — that he looked better than anyone who had tried.
etymology: Italian, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in 'The Book of the Courtier' (1528), from 'sprezzare' (to disdain); literally 'studied carelessness'.

definition: A leisurely stroller who wanders the city to observe and absorb its life.
exampleSentence: He spent the afternoon as a flâneur, drifting through the arcades with no destination in mind.
etymology: From French 'flâner' (to stroll); raised from a pejorative for an idler into an artistic ideal by Charles Baudelaire in the 1860s.

definition: An excessive desire to stay in bed.
exampleSentence: On dark January mornings her clinomania was almost a medical condition.
etymology: From Greek 'kline' (bed) + 'mania' (madness, craving).

definition: A fine, drifting drizzle so light it seems to hang in the air rather than fall.
exampleSentence: A grey smirr hung over the glen, soaking them without ever quite raining.
etymology: Scots, recorded from 1808; origin obscure, perhaps related to Dutch/Low German 'smoren' (to smother, smoke).

definition: A brief glimpse, or a fleeting gleam of light.
exampleSentence: She caught only a glisk of the deer before it melted back into the trees.
etymology: Scots; related to Norwegian dialect 'glisa' (to gleam) and Old English 'glisian' (to glitter), with a frequentative '-k'.

definition: A sudden, violent squall of cold wind sweeping down from a mountainous coast to the sea.
exampleSentence: A williwaw came roaring off the headland and laid the little yacht almost flat.
etymology: Of uncertain origin; a British seamen's word from the mid-19th century, associated with the Strait of Magellan and the Aleutian Islands.

definition: The act or habit of talking in one's sleep.
exampleSentence: His somniloquy was so vivid that she once held a whole conversation with him while he slept.
etymology: From Latin 'somnus' (sleep) + 'loqui' (to speak), modelled on 'soliloquy'; 19th century.

definition: A nosy busybody who must know all the latest gossip.
exampleSentence: The village quidnunc had the news of the engagement before the couple had told their parents.
etymology: From Latin 'quid nunc' (what now?); first used in English in 1709 by Richard Steele in 'The Tatler'.

definition: Of a sound: loud, resonant, and mournful.
exampleSentence: The plangent toll of the buoy bell carried across the dark water.
etymology: From Latin 'plangere' (to strike, beat the breast, lament); early 19th century.

definition: Full of flavour; tasty — and, figuratively, engaging or lively.
exampleSentence: After weeks of bland hospital food, the sapid little stew tasted like a celebration.
etymology: From Latin 'sapidus' (savoury), from 'sapere' (to taste, have flavour); 17th century.

definition: To lie in bed or lounge about long after you should have got up.
exampleSentence: It was a grey Sunday made for nothing but coffee and a long hurkle-durkle.
etymology: Scots rhyming reduplication built on 'hurkle' (to crouch, draw the limbs together); recorded in John Jamieson's dictionary of Scots (Supplement, 1825).

definition: A narrow path or alleyway running between two walls or hedges.
exampleSentence: They cut home through a twitten barely wide enough for one.
etymology: Sussex dialect, recorded in W. D. Parish's Dictionary of the Sussex Dialect (1875) and the OED; perhaps related to Old English 'twicen', a place where two roads meet.

definition: Lavish, extravagant spending on food and drink.
exampleSentence: A weekend of oysters and champagne was pure abligurition.
etymology: From Latin 'abligurire' (to squander on delicacies), from 'ab-' (away) + 'ligurire' (to be dainty), from 'lingere' (to lick). Entered English via Nathan Bailey's 1724 dictionary, defined as 'A prodigal spending in Belly-Cheer'.

definition: To wander or roam idly and aimlessly.
exampleSentence: We spent the afternoon stravaiging through the old town.
etymology: Scots, probably an aphetic form of 'extravage', from Medieval Latin 'extravagari' (to wander beyond limits), per the Dictionary of the Scots Language; used by Burns and Hogg.

definition: Spray blown from the crests of waves by a gale; also fine wind-driven snow.
exampleSentence: Spindrift streamed off the breakers in a salt haze.
etymology: Scots formation (c.1600), of uncertain origin; OED links it to 'spoondrift', from 'spoon/spoom' (to sail before the wind) + 'drift'. Popularized in English by novelist William Black (1841–1898).

definition: The bright track of moonlight reflected across water.
exampleSentence: A moonglade lay across the bay like a silver road.
etymology: American English compound of 'moon' + 'glade' (a bright open patch). OED's earliest evidence is 1867, in the writing of James Russell Lowell.

definition: Of or occurring in the dark hours just before dawn.
exampleSentence: They set off in the antelucan hush, before the birds woke.
etymology: From Latin 'antelucanus', from 'ante-' (before) + 'lux, luc-' (light); earliest English use early 17th century.

definition: The fading half-light of dusk; twilight.
exampleSentence: We watched the valley dissolve into the dimpsy.
etymology: West Country (Devon/Somerset) dialect, of uncertain origin; probably from 'dim'. Compare local 'dimmit'/'dumpsey'.

definition: Emerald-green; of or relating to emeralds.
exampleSentence: The lake shone a deep smaragdine under the pines.
etymology: From Latin 'smaragdinus', from Greek 'smaragdos' (emerald); first English use 1382 (Wycliffite Bible).

definition: The strong smell of cooking or burning meat or fat.
exampleSentence: The nidor of the roasting goose filled the house.
etymology: From Latin 'nidor' (a steam, fumes, strong smell), of uncertain origin.

definition: (Of the stomach) to rumble and churn with nausea; to move unsteadily.
exampleSentence: My stomach wambled after the ferry crossing.
etymology: Late Middle English, of uncertain origin; compare Danish 'vamle' (to feel queasy).

definition: A tightrope walker.
exampleSentence: The funambulist crossed between the towers without a net.
etymology: From Latin 'funis' (rope) + 'ambulare' (to walk).

definition: Idle daydreaming; absent-minded indulgence in fancy.
exampleSentence: Caught woolgathering, she missed the question entirely.
etymology: From the literal gathering of stray tufts of wool from hedges — a trivial, wandering errand; figurative sense from the 16th century.

definition: A person who scavenges in river mud at low tide for objects of value.
exampleSentence: The mudlark surfaced with a clay pipe and a Tudor coin.
etymology: From 'mud' + 'lark' (in the sense of a frolic); first recorded 1780s on the Thames.

definition: A foolish, absent-minded or gullible person.
exampleSentence: Don't stand there like a mooncalf — help me lift it.
etymology: From 'moon' + 'calf', from the old belief the moon caused abnormal births; sense 'simpleton' from the 1620s. OED earliest 1565.

definition: An incorrigible, habitual rascal.
exampleSentence: Her youngest was a charming scapegrace who never paid a debt.
etymology: From 'scape' (archaic for 'escape') + 'grace' — literally 'one who has escaped the grace of God'. Merriam-Webster dates first use to 1763; OED's earliest cite is 1809.

definition: To rain in very fine, misty drops.
exampleSentence: It mizzled all morning, too soft to call rain.
etymology: Late Middle English 'misellen', of obscure origin; compare Dutch dialect 'miezelen' (to drizzle).

definition: The rosy glow on mountain summits just before sunrise or after sunset.
exampleSentence: The peaks burned pink with alpenglow as the sun dropped.
etymology: Partial calque of German 'Alpenglühen' (Alpen 'Alps' + Glühen 'glow'); OED's earliest evidence is 1862, in a letter by W. H. Brewer.

definition: A soft, gentle breeze, especially from the west.
exampleSentence: A zephyr stirred the curtains on the warm afternoon.
etymology: From Latin 'Zephyrus', from Greek 'Zephyros', the personified west wind; 'gentle breeze' sense c.1600.

definition: To look amorously or longingly at someone.
exampleSentence: He smickered at her across the crowded room.
etymology: Scots and dialect English; related to obsolete 'smicker' meaning elegant, amorous.

definition: The traditional collective noun for a flight of larks.
exampleSentence: An exaltation of larks rose singing from the meadow.
etymology: From Latin 'exaltare' (to raise high); the bird sense is listed in the Book of St Albans (1486) as 'an Exaltynge of larkys'.

definition: A great wheeling flock of starlings; a low murmuring sound.
exampleSentence: A murmuration of starlings rippled across the dusk sky.
etymology: From Latin 'murmurare' (to murmur); the starling-flock sense recorded among the collective nouns of the late medieval period.

definition: The dappled, shifting sunlight that filters through the leaves of trees.
exampleSentence: We lay on the moss and watched the komorebi tremble gold across our hands.
etymology: Japanese 木漏れ日, from 木 'ko' (tree) + 漏れ 'more' (leaking through) + 日 'bi' (sunlight); literally 'sunlight that leaks through trees'.

definition: The excess weight gained from comfort-eating one's way through grief or stress.
exampleSentence: Three months of breakup ice cream left him with a soft layer of kummerspeck.
etymology: German, from 'Kummer' (grief) + 'Speck' (bacon, fat); literally 'grief bacon'. Recorded in the Collins German–English Dictionary.

definition: The seemingly malicious behaviour of inanimate objects that conspire to thwart us.
exampleSentence: The printer jamming five minutes before the deadline was pure resistentialism.
etymology: Coined in 1948 by humorist Paul Jennings in 'Report on Resistentialism' (The Spectator); a blend of Latin 'res' (thing) + French 'résister' + 'existentialism', spoofing Sartre. Slogan: 'Les choses sont contre nous'.

definition: The rush of joy felt on reuniting with someone after a long time apart.
exampleSentence: The airport arrivals hall was a sea of tearful retrouvailles and crushed bouquets.
etymology: French, from 'retrouver' (to find again); literally 'rediscoveries', the happiness of meeting again.

definition: A gullible person who will credulously swallow whatever they are told.
exampleSentence: Every conspiracy thread found a fresh gobemouche ready to believe and repost it.
etymology: French, from 'gober' (to gulp down) + 'mouche' (fly); literally a 'fly-swallower', mouth hanging open. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Stoic inner grit that keeps you going long after reason says to quit.
exampleSentence: It took pure sisu to finish the marathon on a sprained ankle in the sleet.
etymology: Finnish, from 'sisus' (the insides, the gut); a near-mythic Finnish ideal of resolve in adversity.

definition: The intuitive art of reading a room and sensing others' unspoken moods.
exampleSentence: She had the nunchi to change the subject the instant the table went quiet.
etymology: Korean 눈치, from 'nun' (eye); literally 'eye-measure', the quick gauging of a situation through subtle cues.

definition: Warmly friendly, kindly and snugly comfortable, of a person or place.
exampleSentence: The wee couthie pub welcomed us in from the rain with a roaring fire.
etymology: Scots, from 'couth' (known, familiar, kindly); the opposite of the now-common 'uncouth'. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: To do nothing on purpose, idling without aim or guilt.
exampleSentence: On Sundays she simply niksens by the window, watching the street go by.
etymology: Dutch, from 'niks' (nothing); the deliberate, restorative practice of doing nothing at all.

definition: The act of rising at dawn and going outside expressly to hear the first birdsong of the morning.
exampleSentence: We set an alarm for four and slipped into the garden for a gökotta before anyone else woke.
etymology: Swedish, from 'gök' (cuckoo) + 'otta' (the early hours before dawn, from Old Norse 'ótta'); a tradition linked to Ascension Day, documented in The Local's guide to Swedish life.

definition: The glowing pride and joy you feel at the achievements of someone you love, especially a child.
exampleSentence: Watching her daughter conduct the orchestra, she felt a wave of naches she could barely contain.
etymology: Yiddish 'nakhes', from Hebrew 'naḥath' (contentment); listed in Merriam-Webster and the OED among naturalized Yiddish borrowings.

definition: A sudden brief shiver of excitement or thrill that ripples through you.
exampleSentence: When the choir hit the final chord, a frisson ran straight up the back of her neck.
etymology: French for 'shiver', from Late Latin 'friction-, frictio', taken as a derivative of 'frigēre' (to be cold); defined by Merriam-Webster as 'a sudden strong feeling of excitement or fear'.

definition: A livestream or video in which the host eats a huge quantity of food while chatting to viewers.
exampleSentence: She unwound after exams by watching a noodle mukbang, oddly soothed by the slurping and gossip.
etymology: Korean blend of 'meokda' (to eat) + 'bangsong' (broadcast); per the OED, its earliest evidence is from 2013, added in the September 2021 Korean update.

definition: A dreamy daze or trance in which you drift far from what is in front of you.
exampleSentence: He stared out at the rain and slid into a dwam, missing his name being called twice.
etymology: Scots, related to Old English 'dwolma' (chaos, confusion) and Old Saxon 'dwalm' (delusion); attested from the 16th century in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: A noisy uproar, squabble, or general commotion.
exampleSentence: A burst pipe at midnight set off a glorious stramash of buckets, shouting, and slamming doors.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain origin; recorded in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language from 1803 meaning 'an uproar, commotion, hubbub'.

definition: A person dogged by chronic bad luck, the one the spilled soup always lands on.
exampleSentence: Poor schlimazel — he finally bought an umbrella, and that was the week of the drought.
etymology: Yiddish 'shlimazl', from Middle High German 'slim' (crooked) + Hebrew 'mazzāl' (luck); in Merriam-Webster, contrasted with the bungling 'schlemiel'.

definition: A snatch of music that lodges in your head and replays itself against your will.
exampleSentence: One advert jingle became such an earworm that she hummed it absent-mindedly for three days.
etymology: A 1980s loan-translation of German 'Ohrwurm' ('ear' + 'worm'); defined by Merriam-Webster as 'a song or melody that keeps repeating in one's mind'.

definition: A hug that wraps you in warmth and safety; also a snug little cubbyhole.
exampleSentence: After the bad news she just wanted a long cwtch from her mam and nothing more.
etymology: Welsh, thought to derive from Old French 'couche' (a resting or hiding place); listed in Collins meaning both a cuddle and a cubbyhole.

definition: The warm, cosy, good-natured cheer of a snug and friendly gathering.
exampleSentence: Candlelight, mulled wine, and old friends gave the little cabin an unmistakable gemütlichkeit.
etymology: German, from 'gemütlich' (cosy, agreeable), from 'Gemüt' (mind, heart); Merriam-Webster defines it as 'cordiality, friendliness'.

definition: Pompous, wordy language so tangled it becomes unintelligible.
exampleSentence: The contract was forty pages of legal gobbledygook nobody on the team could actually parse.
etymology: Coined by US Congressman Maury Maverick in a memo of 30 March 1944 banning the bureaucratic style; he said it evoked a turkey's pompous 'gobble'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A charming, amusing first encounter that sparks a future romance.
exampleSentence: They had a perfect meet-cute, both reaching for the last copy of the same battered paperback.
etymology: From the screenwriting phrase 'to meet cute', familiar in Hollywood by 1941; the OED and Merriam-Webster record the noun from 1952.

definition: To swell with delighted pride, especially over someone you love.
exampleSentence: Grandpa couldn't stop kvelling when the baby took her first wobbling steps across the kitchen.
etymology: Yiddish 'kveln' (to be delighted), from Middle High German 'quellen' (to well or gush); in Merriam-Webster, with earliest English print evidence from 1952.

definition: To spruce something up with a small, finishing tweak that completes the look.
exampleSentence: She zhuzhed the plain table with a runner and a jug of wildflowers before the guests arrived.
etymology: An imitative word popularised in styling and drag culture; added by Merriam-Webster on 27 September 2023 in a batch of 690 new words, defined as a small improvement that completes the overall look.

definition: To snuggle in close and cosy, nestling against someone or something warm.
exampleSentence: On stormy nights the children would coorie into the big armchair under one shared blanket.
etymology: Scots, a diminutive of 'coor' (to cower or crouch); recorded in the Dictionaries of the Scots Language and in Collins as 'to nestle or snuggle'.

definition: To cheat or hoodwink someone with a brazen bit of trickery.
exampleSentence: The smooth salesman tried to hornswoggle them into buying a roof they plainly didn't need.
etymology: A fanciful American coinage of obscure origin, dating to about 1829; defined in Merriam-Webster as 'to deceive' or 'bamboozle'.

definition: To understand something so deeply and intuitively that you seem to merge with it.
exampleSentence: It took weeks before she truly grokked the new system rather than just following the steps.
etymology: Coined by Robert A. Heinlein in his 1961 novel 'Stranger in a Strange Land' as a Martian word literally meaning 'to drink'; in Merriam-Webster and the OED.

definition: So choked up with emotion that you can barely speak.
exampleSentence: Reading her late father's letter aloud, she got too verklempt to finish the final line.
etymology: Yiddish 'farklemt' (depressed, gripped), from a Germanic root meaning 'to press or squeeze'; popularised by a 1990s sketch-comedy character and listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Looking pale, wan, and a bit off-colour.
exampleSentence: You're awful peely-wally this morning — away back to bed and I'll bring soup.
etymology: Scots, a reduplicated form linked to 'pale' and the sickly sense of 'peelie' (attested 1808); in Collins and the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Ridiculous, implausible, and not to be taken seriously.
exampleSentence: He had some cockamamie scheme to get rich selling ice to penguins.
etymology: American English, attested by 1946; probably an alteration of 'decalcomania' via the children's transfer-tattoos once called 'cockamamies'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Glowingly pleased and delighted with how something has turned out.
exampleSentence: She was dead chuffed when her little garden won a ribbon at the village show.
etymology: British informal, from dialectal 'chuff' (pleased, puffed up with pride); defined in Collins as very pleased.

definition: Utterly astonished, as if struck speechless in the mouth.
exampleSentence: We were gobsmacked when the quiet kid from the back row won the national prize.
etymology: British, from 'gob' (slang for mouth, of Celtic origin) + 'smacked'; in Collins and the OED, with an earliest citation from 1935.

definition: Irritable and short-tempered as a direct result of being hungry.
exampleSentence: Feed him before the meeting or he'll get hangry and snap at the whole room.
etymology: A portmanteau of 'hungry' and 'angry'; added to Merriam-Webster in September 2018, defined as 'irritable or angry because of hunger'.

definition: Set askew or diagonally; out of true alignment.
exampleSentence: The earthquake left every picture in the hall hanging cattywampus.
etymology: 19th-century American English of uncertain origin, probably from 'cater' (diagonal, from French 'quatre') plus a fanciful element; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: In hopeless, jumbled disorder.
exampleSentence: The books were stacked higgledy-piggledy, fiction and physics toppling into one another.
etymology: A 16th-century rhyming reduplication, probably alluding to the jostling of pigs huddling together; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A very small amount; a mere trace or hint.
exampleSentence: Add just a soupçon of nutmeg, or the custard will taste medicinal.
etymology: From French 'soupcon' (suspicion), from Latin 'suspectio'; naturalised into English and listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small stimulus or boost that revives interest or energy.
exampleSentence: The surprise bonus gave the whole team a much-needed fillip.
etymology: Probably imitative of the sound of a finger flicked off a thumb; a Merriam-Webster headword from the 16th century.

definition: A confused, complicated, and embarrassing situation.
exampleSentence: He was dragged into a legal imbroglio that took years to untangle.
etymology: From Italian 'imbroglio', from 'imbrogliare' (to entangle, confuse); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: A situation that is comprehensively and chaotically mismanaged.
exampleSentence: The launch was an omnishambles of crashed servers and contradictory emails.
etymology: Coined for the BBC satire 'The Thick of It' (2009), from Latin 'omni-' (all) + 'shambles'; added to the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Vigour, vivacity, and lively spirit.
exampleSentence: She played the final movement with such brio that the audience leapt up.
etymology: From Italian (and Spanish) 'brio' (liveliness, vigour); borrowed into English and listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Composure and coolness under pressure or danger.
exampleSentence: He defused the argument with remarkable sangfroid and a single dry joke.
etymology: From French 'sang-froid' (cold blood), from 'sang' (blood) + 'froid' (cold); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Cheerful, good-natured friendliness.
exampleSentence: The host's easy bonhomie soon put the nervous guests at their ease.
etymology: From French 'bonhomie', from 'bonhomme' (good-natured man), from 'bon' (good) + 'homme' (man); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A person skilled at telling stories in an entertaining way.
exampleSentence: Our uncle was a born raconteur who could make a grocery run sound epic.
etymology: From French 'raconteur', from 'raconter' (to relate, tell); naturalised into English and in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A flamboyant charlatan who deceives people for money or fame.
exampleSentence: The so-called doctor was a mountebank peddling coloured water as a cure.
etymology: From Italian 'montimbanco' (one who mounts a bench to hawk wares), from 'montare in banco'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A wasteful, idle, good-for-nothing person.
exampleSentence: He squandered the inheritance like a true wastrel and was broke by spring.
etymology: From English 'waste' + the noun suffix '-rel'; a Merriam-Webster headword from the 19th century.

definition: A vain, talkative person given to showing off.
exampleSentence: The young popinjay spent more on his cravats than on his rent.
etymology: Originally meaning 'parrot', from Old French 'papegai', ultimately of Arabic origin; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A person devoted to luxury and sensual pleasure.
exampleSentence: A confirmed sybarite, he judged every hotel by the softness of its towels.
etymology: From 'Sybaris', an ancient Greek colony in Italy famed for the luxury of its citizens; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A state of nervous restlessness, irritability, or unease.
exampleSentence: Crowded lifts give me the fantods, so I always take the stairs.
etymology: Of obscure 19th-century origin, perhaps related to 'fantastic'; a Merriam-Webster headword, often used as 'the fantods'.

definition: A fit of intense indignation or resentment.
exampleSentence: He stormed out in high dudgeon when his idea was politely dismissed.
etymology: Of unknown origin, recorded since the 16th century, usually in the phrase 'in high dudgeon'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Dark, shadowy, and gloomy.
exampleSentence: They groped down a tenebrous stair that smelled of damp stone.
etymology: From Latin 'tenebrae' (darkness, shadows); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Transparently clear, whether in substance or in expression.
exampleSentence: Her pellucid prose made even quantum theory feel almost simple.
etymology: From Latin 'pellucidus', from 'per-' (through) + 'lucere' (to shine); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Strange and sinister in an eerie, otherworldly way.
exampleSentence: An eldritch wail drifted up from the empty well at midnight.
etymology: A Scots word of uncertain origin, perhaps from 'elf' + an old word for realm; honestly its roots are debated. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Disreputable or shady, yet somehow appealing.
exampleSentence: The bar had a louche, velvet-curtained charm that respectable people pretended to ignore.
etymology: From French 'louche' (squinting, cross-eyed), from Latin 'luscus' (one-eyed); the sense drifted to 'shady'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Casually carefree and unconcerned.
exampleSentence: He gave an insouciant shrug, as if the missed flight meant nothing.
etymology: From French 'insouciant', from 'in-' (not) + 'soucier' (to trouble, care); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To care for and indulge with excessive tenderness.
exampleSentence: They cosset that little dog as though it were visiting royalty.
etymology: From the noun 'cosset' (a pet lamb raised by hand), of uncertain earlier origin; a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To move along heavily and clumsily.
exampleSentence: The puppy galumphed across the lawn, ears flapping wildly.
etymology: Coined by Lewis Carroll in 'Jabberwocky' (1871), probably blending 'gallop' and 'triumph'; now in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Soon; in a short time.
exampleSentence: Wait here by the gate, and I shall return anon.
etymology: From Old English 'on an' (in one, at once); a Merriam-Webster headword, now chiefly literary or archaic.

definition: Swiftly; at a quick pace.
exampleSentence: With the deadline looming, the work proceeded apace.
etymology: From Middle English, from the phrase 'a pas' (at a pace), via Anglo-French; a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: With a sideways glance of suspicion or disapproval.
exampleSentence: The locals eyed the newcomers askance until the first round of drinks.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, recorded from the 16th century; a Merriam-Webster headword, often in 'look askance'.

definition: Empty flattery or pretentious nonsense dressed up as substance.
exampleSentence: The keynote was pure flummery, forty minutes of buzzwords and no single concrete idea.
etymology: From Welsh 'llymru' (a soured oatmeal jelly); a Collins and Merriam-Webster headword, the figurative 'empty talk' sense recorded by Lady Luxborough in a 1749 letter.

definition: An utter, spiritless coward.
exampleSentence: The general called the deserters poltroons who had abandoned braver men to die.
etymology: From Old Italian 'poltrone' (coward), via Middle French; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, attested in English before 1529 in John Skelton.

definition: A small unexpected gift or extra given as a gesture of goodwill.
exampleSentence: The baker slipped a warm cruller into the bag as a lagniappe.
etymology: From Louisiana French, from American Spanish 'la ñapa', ultimately Quechua 'yapa' (something added); a Merriam-Webster headword celebrated by Mark Twain in 'Life on the Mississippi' (1883) as 'a word worth travelling to New Orleans to get.'

definition: A trace of an earlier image showing through the surface of a painting.
exampleSentence: A faint pentimento revealed the hand the artist had painted out years before.
etymology: From Italian 'pentimento' (repentance), from 'pentirsi' (to repent); a Merriam-Webster and Collins headword, first used in English in 1823.

definition: Good-natured teasing or witty banter that pokes fun without malice.
exampleSentence: The dinner dissolved into affectionate raillery about his disastrous cooking.
etymology: From French 'raillerie', from 'railler' (to mock); a Merriam-Webster headword, in English from the 1650s.

definition: Something that brings sweet forgetfulness of sorrow or pain.
exampleSentence: Sleep was the only nepenthe she could find after the long, grieving spring.
etymology: From Greek 'nepenthes', from 'ne-' (not) + 'penthos' (grief); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, in English from the late 1500s.

definition: A flighty, frivolous, excessively chattering person.
exampleSentence: She adored her aunt, a cheerful flibbertigibbet who could not keep a secret for an hour.
etymology: From Middle English 'flepergebet', an onomatopoeic imitation of meaningless chatter; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword attested before 1450.

definition: Offence or resentment taken at a perceived slight.
exampleSentence: He took umbrage at being seated below the salt at his own brother's wedding.
etymology: From Latin 'umbra' (shade, shadow), via Old French; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, the 'offence' sense dating to the 1600s.

definition: An item of food; something fit to be eaten.
exampleSentence: They laid out every comestible the pantry could yield for the unexpected guests.
etymology: From Late Latin 'comestibilis', from Latin 'comedere' (to eat up); a Merriam-Webster and Collins headword.

definition: A bad-tempered, surly, often miserly person.
exampleSentence: The old curmudgeon next door confiscated any ball that crossed his fence.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, attested in English from the late 1500s; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword whose etymology is honestly unknown.

definition: Charming in a fresh, innocent, and engaging way.
exampleSentence: She had a winsome habit of laughing at her own jokes before the punchline.
etymology: From Old English 'wynsum', from 'wynn' (joy, delight) + '-sum'; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: Everyday; commonplace and recurring daily.
exampleSentence: She found a strange beauty in quotidian things: bus tickets, kettles, rain.
etymology: From Latin 'quotidianus', from 'quotidie' (every day); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: Exquisitely delicious or fragrant, as if fit for the gods.
exampleSentence: The ambrosial smell of ripe peaches filled the whole sun-warmed orchard.
etymology: From Greek 'ambrosia' (food of the gods), from 'a-' (not) + 'brotos' (mortal); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To speak or write at pompous, windy, empty length.
exampleSentence: He bloviated for an hour about leadership without defining a single term.
etymology: American English, probably from 'blow' plus a mock-Latin ending; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword first recorded in 1845 (and popularised under President Warren G. Harding).

definition: To dance clumsily, with more joy than grace.
exampleSentence: By midnight the whole wedding was baltering across the lawn, shoes long abandoned.
etymology: From Middle English 'balteren', of North Germanic origin; an archaic Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To worry or be burdened with anxious care.
exampleSentence: Stop carking over the harvest; the rain will come or it won't.
etymology: From Middle English 'carken' (to be anxious), from Old English; an archaic Merriam-Webster and Collins headword.

definition: To bewitch or enchant utterly.
exampleSentence: The violinist ensorcelled the hall until not a programme rustled.
etymology: From Middle French 'ensorceler', from 'sorcier' (sorcerer); a Merriam-Webster, Collins and OED headword (also spelled 'ensorcel').

definition: Strongly smelling of something; evocative of a fragrance.
exampleSentence: The kitchen was redolent of cinnamon and cloves.
etymology: From Latin 'redolere' to emit a scent.

definition: The state of being infatuated and obsessively preoccupied with another person.
exampleSentence: His limerence faded once the relationship became routine.
etymology: Coined in the 1970s by psychologist Dorothy Tennov.

definition: A state of listlessness and spiritual apathy; torpor of the soul.
exampleSentence: A profound acedia kept him from any meaningful work.
etymology: From Greek 'akedia' meaning lack of care.

definition: A state of serene calmness and freedom from emotional disturbance.
exampleSentence: The philosopher sought ataraxia through detachment.
etymology: From Greek 'ataraxia' meaning impassiveness, calm.

definition: A soft murmuring or rustling sound; a whisper.
exampleSentence: A susurrus of leaves filled the quiet wood.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrus' meaning a humming, whisper.

definition: Something that brings a final end or release; a settling.
exampleSentence: The scandal put the quietus on his political career.
etymology: From Latin 'quietus est' meaning he is quit, discharged.

definition: The act of throwing someone or something out of a window; by extension, a swift removal from power.
exampleSentence: The board meeting ended in a quiet defenestration: by Friday the founder's name was already gone from the door.
etymology: From Latin 'de-' (down from) + 'fenestra' (window); coined around the Second Defenestration of Prague (23 May 1618), when Protestant nobles threw two regents ~70 feet from a castle window, sparking the Thirty Years' War.

definition: A misheard word or phrase, especially in a song, that yields a new meaning.
exampleSentence: For years he belted 'wrapped up like a douche' into his hairbrush - a mondegreen he refused to give up even after learning the real line.
etymology: Coined by Sylvia Wright in 'The Death of Lady Mondegreen' (Harper's, November 1954), after she misheard the ballad line 'laid him on the green' as 'Lady Mondegreen.'

definition: A sudden, joyous turn for the good at the darkest point of a story.
exampleSentence: Right when the city seemed lost, the horns sounded on the hill - a perfect eucatastrophe.
etymology: Coined by J. R. R. Tolkien (from a 1939 St Andrews lecture, published 1947 in 'Essays Presented to Charles Williams'): 'Since we do not appear to possess a word... I will call it Eucatastrophe,' from Greek 'eu-' (good) + 'catastrophe' (sudden turn).

definition: The scented trail left lingering in the air after a perfumed person passes.
exampleSentence: She had already turned the corner, but her sillage hung in the stairwell like a signature.
etymology: From French 'sillage' (the wake of a ship), from 'sillon' (furrow), ultimately from Latin 'secare' (to cut).

definition: Glittering with gold or tinsel; showily brilliant.
exampleSentence: The ballroom was clinquant with chandeliers, every surface throwing back light.
etymology: From French 'clinquant,' present participle of the obsolete 'clinquer' (to clink, glitter), of imitative origin.

definition: A deep, wistful longing for a home or past that may never have existed; bittersweet homesickness for the irrecoverable.
exampleSentence: Hearing the old language on the train platform filled her with hiraeth for a village she had never actually lived in.
etymology: A Welsh word with no exact English equivalent, blending grief and longing for the lost or the never-was.

definition: A wish or inclination so slight it prompts no action whatsoever.
exampleSentence: He had a velleity to learn the cello - enough to admire one in a shop window, never enough to buy it.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'velleitas,' from Latin 'velle' (to wish, to will).

definition: Of or resembling twilight; (of animals) active mainly at dawn and dusk.
exampleSentence: Deer are crepuscular, so the meadow filled with them only as the light began to fail.
etymology: From Latin 'crepusculum' (twilight), from 'creper' (dusky, obscure).

definition: Feeling the presence of something holy, awe-inspiring and beyond comprehension.
exampleSentence: Standing alone in the vast empty cathedral, she felt something numinous she had no church for.
etymology: From Latin 'numen' (divine will, the nod of a god); given its modern sense by theologian Rudolf Otto in 1917.

definition: The emission of light when certain materials are rubbed, crushed, or torn apart.
exampleSentence: Crushing a wintergreen sweet in the dark can spark a faint blue triboluminescence.
etymology: Borrowed from German Triboluminescenz, from Greek tribein 'to rub' plus luminescence; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A glassy tube or crust formed when lightning fuses sand or rock.
exampleSentence: After the storm they unearthed a fragile fulgurite where lightning had struck the dune.
etymology: Borrowed from German Fulgurit, from Latin fulgur 'lightning'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A comic four-line biographical poem rhyming AABB that names its subject in the first line.
exampleSentence: She dashed off a clerihew mocking the headmaster's love of Latin.
etymology: Named after Edmund Clerihew Bentley, who invented it as a bored schoolboy (his first, on Sir Humphry Davy, appeared in 1905) and whose form entered the language as a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An inscription at the end of a book giving facts about its production, or a publisher's emblem.
exampleSentence: The colophon revealed the book was set in Garamond and printed in Verona.
etymology: From Greek kolophon 'summit, finishing touch'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A book printed in Europe before 1501, in the earliest years of the printing press.
exampleSentence: The library guards its sole incunabulum behind climate-controlled glass.
etymology: From Latin incunabula 'swaddling clothes, cradle', from in- plus cunae 'cradle'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To move in a lively, prancing, or exaggerated manner, like a spirited horse.
exampleSentence: The children tittuped down the lane, too excited to walk normally.
etymology: Probably imitative of the sound of hoofbeats; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To move, fly, or sail rapidly, often with a whirring sound.
exampleSentence: Startled grouse skirred low across the moor.
etymology: Perhaps an alteration of 'scour'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An ancient Welsh bowed stringed instrument, a type of lyre.
exampleSentence: At the festival a musician coaxed a haunting drone from a crwth.
etymology: From Welsh crwth, from a Proto-Celtic word for 'round object'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Twilight; the dim half-light just after sunset or before sunrise.
exampleSentence: We lingered on the porch through the violet crepuscule.
etymology: From Latin crepusculum 'twilight', from creper 'dusky'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Wavelike ridges of hard snow carved by the wind on a snowfield.
exampleSentence: The skiers rattled across endless sastrugi on the polar plateau.
etymology: From German, from dialectal Russian zastruga 'groove, small ridge'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Fine rain falling from an apparently cloudless sky, typically after sunset.
exampleSentence: A soft serein dampened the courtyard though not a cloud was in sight.
etymology: From French serein 'evening', from Latin serum 'a late hour'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Full of twists, turns, and windings; tortuous.
exampleSentence: We followed an anfractuous trail through the gorge.
etymology: From Late Latin anfractuosus, from amb- 'around' plus frangere 'to break'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A person learning the rudiments of something, especially the alphabet; a beginner.
exampleSentence: In calligraphy she remained a cheerful abecedarian, still mastering her letters.
etymology: From Late Latin abecedarius, formed from the letters a, b, c, d; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To leap upward with all four legs stiff and straight, as a springbok does.
exampleSentence: The young springbok began to pronk joyfully across the veld.
etymology: From Afrikaans pronk 'to show off, strut'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: To glide downward through the air without engine power.
exampleSentence: The pilot cut the motor and let the biplane volplane toward the meadow.
etymology: From French vol plane 'gliding flight'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A light leap by a horse in which all four feet briefly leave the ground.
exampleSentence: The stallion performed an elegant curvet before the crowd.
etymology: From Italian corvetta, diminutive of corva 'curve'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An upward leap by a trained horse that kicks its hind legs out without moving forward.
exampleSentence: The Lipizzaner executed a flawless capriole during the exhibition.
etymology: From Italian capriola 'a leap', from capriolo 'roebuck'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A spring or leap of a horse; also a caper or playful antic.
exampleSentence: The colt made a sudden gambado, nearly unseating its rider.
etymology: From Italian gamba 'leg'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Leaping, jumping, or dancing.
exampleSentence: The heraldic crest showed a saltant stag caught mid-leap.
etymology: From Latin saltare 'to dance, leap'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A tearing or pulling apart; a violent separation.
exampleSentence: The report described the slow divulsion of the two ice sheets.
etymology: From Latin divulsio, from divellere 'to rend apart'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Former; having been such at a previous time.
exampleSentence: She ran into her whilom colleague at the conference.
etymology: From Old English hwilum 'at times', dative plural of hwil 'while'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Yesterday evening; last night.
exampleSentence: We danced together yestreen beneath the harvest moon.
etymology: From Middle English yestreen, from Old English elements meaning 'yesterday evening'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Of or occurring in the month preceding the present one.
exampleSentence: Your letter of the 12th ultimo has been received.
etymology: From Latin ultimo mense 'in the last month'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A timekeeping device such as a clock or sundial.
exampleSentence: An ancient horologe still marked the hours in the abbey tower.
etymology: From Latin horologium, from Greek hora 'hour' plus legein 'to gather'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The day after tomorrow.
exampleSentence: If we leave overmorrow, we will arrive before the festival ends.
etymology: From Middle English overmorwe (over- plus morrow); a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A while before; formerly; some time ago.
exampleSentence: The garden, erewhile neglected, now bloomed with roses.
etymology: From Old English aer 'before' plus while; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An abnormal lack of ability to act or make decisions.
exampleSentence: His abulia left him paralyzed before even the simplest choices.
etymology: From New Latin, from Greek a- 'without' plus boule 'will'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A transformative change of heart, especially a spiritual conversion.
exampleSentence: His year abroad sparked a profound metanoia that reshaped his values.
etymology: From Greek metanoia 'a change of mind'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Weakness of will; acting against one's own better judgment.
exampleSentence: Reaching for the cigarette, he recognized his akrasia even as he lit it.
etymology: From Greek akrasia 'lack of self-control'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The investment of mental or emotional energy in a person, object, or idea.
exampleSentence: Her cathexis toward the old house bordered on obsession.
etymology: From New Latin, from Greek kathexis 'holding'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Purely intellectual apprehension; the highest form of knowing.
exampleSentence: Plato prized noesis as the soul's grasp of eternal forms.
etymology: From Greek noesis 'understanding', from noein 'to think'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The subjective, felt qualities of conscious experience, such as the redness of red.
exampleSentence: Philosophers debate whether a machine could ever experience qualia.
etymology: Latin plural of quale 'of what kind'; a headword in the American Heritage Dictionary.

definition: Social instability and personal alienation from a breakdown of shared standards and values.
exampleSentence: The collapse of the industry left the town gripped by anomie.
etymology: From French, from Greek anomos 'lawless'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Courteous and friendly social or political harmony among groups.
exampleSentence: The treaty restored a measure of comity between the rival nations.
etymology: From Latin comitas 'courtesy', from comis 'courteous'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A fellowship or association of people sharing a common interest or devotion.
exampleSentence: She joined the parish sodality devoted to charitable work.
etymology: From Latin sodalitas, from sodalis 'companion'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The general welfare; the good of the whole community.
exampleSentence: The reforms were enacted for the commonweal rather than private gain.
etymology: From Middle English commune 'common' plus wele 'well-being'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A bright, often colored spot beside the sun caused by ice crystals; a sun dog.
exampleSentence: A brilliant parhelion glowed to the left of the winter sun.
etymology: From Greek parelion (para- 'beside' plus helios 'sun'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A complex mirage that distorts distant objects, often seen over water.
exampleSentence: On the horizon a fata morgana raised phantom cliffs above the sea.
etymology: Italian for 'Morgan the Fairy', after the enchantress Morgan le Fay blamed for the mirage of the Strait of Messina; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Sunlight reflected by the earth that faintly illuminates the dark part of the moon.
exampleSentence: Earthshine lit the shadowed crescent with a soft silver glow.
etymology: From earth plus shine, the effect Leonardo da Vinci first explained around 1510 (the 'Da Vinci Glow'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A diffuse glow in the night sky seen westward after twilight or eastward before dawn.
exampleSentence: From the dark desert we watched the zodiacal light fan up the eastern sky.
etymology: From zodiacal (relating to the zodiac) plus light; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A natural silica glass formed when sand or quartz is fused by lightning or meteorite impact.
exampleSentence: Threads of lechatelierite confirmed that lightning had struck the dune.
etymology: Named after French chemist Henry Le Chatelier; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A magnified shadow of an observer cast onto cloud, often ringed with colored light.
exampleSentence: From the summit she saw her own brocken spectre haloed on the mist below.
etymology: Named after the Brocken, the 1,141 m high point of Germany's Harz Mountains where it was first observed; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: The corner at either side of the eye where the upper and lower lids meet.
exampleSentence: A tear gathered at the inner canthus of her eye.
etymology: From Greek kanthos 'corner of the eye'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The pale, crescent-shaped area at the base of a fingernail.
exampleSentence: The white lunula was just visible at the base of each nail.
etymology: From Latin lunula 'little moon', diminutive of luna; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The big toe, or the innermost digit of the hind foot.
exampleSentence: The runner fractured her hallux during the marathon.
etymology: From New Latin, alteration of Latin allex 'big toe'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The lowest midpoint of the lower jaw, used as an anatomical reference point.
exampleSentence: The anatomist measured from the nasion to the gnathion.
etymology: From Greek gnathos 'jaw'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A volume of writings by various authors presented as a tribute to a scholar.
exampleSentence: Colleagues compiled a festschrift to honor the retiring professor.
etymology: From German Fest 'celebration' plus Schrift 'writing'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A short concluding stanza of a poem, serving as a summary or dedication.
exampleSentence: The ballade ended with a graceful envoi addressed to the prince.
etymology: From Old French envoi 'a sending', from envoyer 'to send'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A song or poem written in honor of a bride and bridegroom.
exampleSentence: The poet composed an epithalamium for the royal wedding.
etymology: From Greek epithalamion (epi- plus thalamos 'bridal chamber'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A poem or song that retracts or recants something said in an earlier one.
exampleSentence: Stesichorus wrote a palinode to take back his insult to Helen.
etymology: From Greek palinoidia (palin 'again' plus aeidein 'to sing'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A literary work, especially a poem, composed entirely of lines borrowed from other authors.
exampleSentence: Her cento stitched together fragments of Virgil into a new poem.
etymology: From Latin cento 'patchwork garment'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A short quotation at the beginning of a book or chapter suggesting its theme.
exampleSentence: The novel opens with an epigraph drawn from Dante.
etymology: From Greek epigraphe 'inscription', from epigraphein 'to write on'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fine network of cracks that forms on the surface of an old painting or varnish.
exampleSentence: Centuries had given the portrait a delicate web of craquelure.
etymology: From French craqueler 'to crackle'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A style of painting using stark contrasts of deep shadow and dramatic light.
exampleSentence: Caravaggio's tenebrism makes the figures emerge from velvet darkness.
etymology: From Italian tenebroso 'dark', from Latin tenebrae 'darkness'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A pose in which a figure's weight rests on one leg, twisting the body's axis.
exampleSentence: Michelangelo's David stands in elegant contrapposto.
etymology: From Italian contrapposto 'set opposite', from Latin contraponere; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The process of coating objects with a hard, glossy black lacquer in the Japanese manner.
exampleSentence: The tray's deep shine came from careful japanning.
etymology: From Japan plus -ing, after Japanese lacquerwork; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to a meal.
exampleSentence: They enjoyed a leisurely post-prandial stroll through the gardens.
etymology: From Latin prandium 'late breakfast, luncheon'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Refreshment by food or drink; a light meal.
exampleSentence: After the long walk they paused for a simple refection of bread and wine.
etymology: From Latin refectio 'restoration', from reficere 'to remake'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Suitable for eating; edible.
exampleSentence: Foragers must distinguish esculent mushrooms from poisonous ones.
etymology: From Latin esculentus 'edible', from esca 'food'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A timid, meek, or unassertive person.
exampleSentence: Everyone expected a milquetoast, but she ran the meeting fearlessly.
etymology: From Caspar Milquetoast, the timid comic-strip soul created by cartoonist H. T. Webster in 1924; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A fashionable, socially active man-about-town.
exampleSentence: A polished boulevardier, he knew every cafe on the avenue.
etymology: From French boulevard, after the Parisian boulevards he frequents; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A play on words; punning.
exampleSentence: Shakespeare's dialogue brims with sly paronomasia.
etymology: From Greek paronomasia 'play on words alike in sound'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A figure of speech in which one word governs two others in different senses.
exampleSentence: The line 'she broke his car and his heart' is a classic zeugma.
etymology: From Greek zeugma 'a joining', from zeugnynai 'to yoke'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The use of a longer, roundabout phrasing instead of a shorter expression.
exampleSentence: The phrase 'at this point in time' is periphrasis for the simple word 'now'.
etymology: From Greek periphrasis (peri- 'around' plus phrazein 'to point out'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A word or phrase borrowed by literally translating its parts; a loan translation.
exampleSentence: The word 'skyscraper' became a calque in many languages through word-for-word translation.
etymology: From French calque 'a copy', from calquer 'to trace'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Raising a subject by claiming you will not mention it.
exampleSentence: By apophasis he reminded everyone of the scandal: "I won't dwell on his bankruptcy."
etymology: From Greek 'apophanai' (to say no), via Late Latin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An abrupt shift to a different grammatical construction within one sentence.
exampleSentence: His speech dissolved into anacoluthon - "I really ought to, well, do as you like."
etymology: From Greek 'anakolouthos' (inconsistent); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repeating the last word of a clause at the start of the next.
exampleSentence: "Fear leads to anger; anger leads to hate" is a textbook anadiplosis.
etymology: From Greek 'anadiplosis' (a doubling back); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Immediate, emphatic repetition of a word for emphasis.
exampleSentence: "Never, never, never give up" is epizeuxis at its most rousing.
etymology: From Greek 'epizeuxis' (a fastening upon); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repeating the same word at the end of successive clauses.
exampleSentence: "Of the people, by the people, for the people" closes each phrase with epistrophe.
etymology: From Greek 'epistrophe' (a turning about); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Omitting conjunctions between a series of related clauses.
exampleSentence: "I came, I saw, I conquered" gains its speed from asyndeton.
etymology: From Greek 'asyndetos' (unconnected); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Deliberate use of many conjunctions in close succession.
exampleSentence: "We have ships and men and money and stores" piles on polysyndeton.
etymology: From Greek 'poly' (many) + 'syndeton' (bound together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repetition of words in successive clauses in reverse order.
exampleSentence: "Eat to live, not live to eat" is a crisp antimetabole.
etymology: From Greek 'antimetabole' (turning about); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sentence whose surprise ending reframes its earlier part.
exampleSentence: "I want to die peacefully like my grandfather, not screaming like his passengers" is pure paraprosdokian.
etymology: From Greek 'para' (contrary to) + 'prosdokia' (expectation); a headword in Dictionary.com.

definition: Repeating the opening word of a clause at its end.
exampleSentence: "The king is dead, long live the king" frames itself with epanalepsis.
etymology: From Greek 'epanalepsis' (a taking up again); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Posing a question then immediately answering it yourself.
exampleSentence: She used hypophora: "What should we do? We should begin at once."
etymology: From Greek 'hypophora' (a carrying under); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: An inverted parallelism in which terms are reversed across clauses.
exampleSentence: "Ask not what your country can do for you" is a famous chiasmus.
etymology: From Greek 'chiasmos' (a crossing), after the letter chi; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Repetition of a word at the beginning of successive clauses.
exampleSentence: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds" rides on anaphora.
etymology: From Greek 'anaphora' (a carrying back); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Expressing one idea with two words linked by 'and'.
exampleSentence: "Nice and warm" is hendiadys for "nicely warm."
etymology: From Greek 'hen dia dyoin' (one through two); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A double reading or twofold interpretation of a text.
exampleSentence: The verse invites dittology, supporting two equally valid readings.
etymology: From Greek 'dittos' (double) + '-logia'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A harsh or blunt term used in place of a milder one.
exampleSentence: Calling a graveyard a "bone yard" is a grim dysphemism.
etymology: From Greek 'dys' (bad) + 'pheme' (speech); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Understatement that affirms something by negating its contrary.
exampleSentence: Saying "she's not bad at chess" about a champion is sly litotes.
etymology: From Greek 'litotes' (plainness), from 'litos' (simple); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Rhetorical understatement that belittles something to make a point.
exampleSentence: Calling a hurricane "a spot of weather" is wry meiosis.
etymology: From Greek 'meiosis' (a lessening); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: One word governing two others in different senses simultaneously.
exampleSentence: "She broke his car and his heart" turns on a neat syllepsis.
etymology: From Greek 'syllepsis' (a taking together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An intense, wistful yearning for something undefined or unattainable.
exampleSentence: The old photograph stirred a deep sehnsucht for a home that no longer existed.
etymology: German 'Sehnen' (yearning) + 'Sucht' (craving); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Pleasure derived from another person's misfortune.
exampleSentence: He watched his rival's downfall with undisguised epicaricacy.
etymology: From Greek 'epi' (upon) + 'chara' (joy) + 'kakon' (evil); recorded as 'epicharikaky' in Nathan Bailey's 1721 Universal Etymological English Dictionary.

definition: Intense, almost overwhelming pleasure or enjoyment.
exampleSentence: There was a reckless jouissance in the way she danced until dawn.
etymology: French 'jouir' (to enjoy), from Latin 'gaudere'; a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: Sorrow, grief, or deep anguish.
exampleSentence: A quiet dolor settled over the house in the weeks after the funeral.
etymology: From Latin 'dolor' (pain, grief); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Anxiety that time is running out to act before opportunities close.
exampleSentence: A wave of torschlusspanik hit him at forty, certain his chances were vanishing.
etymology: German 'Tor' (gate) + 'Schluss' (closing) + 'Panik' (panic); a documented loanword used as the title of a Time Magazine article on 18 August 1961.

definition: Vicarious joy taken in the happiness or success of others.
exampleSentence: Cheering his teammate's win, he felt only mudita, never envy.
etymology: From Pali and Sanskrit 'mudita' (gladness); a documented loanword in English-language Buddhist writing.

definition: Careful, appreciative tasting of food or wine in small portions.
exampleSentence: The restaurant's degustation moved through nine small, exquisite courses.
etymology: From Latin 'degustare' (to taste); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The quality in a substance that produces a sensation of taste.
exampleSentence: The broth had a deep, savory sapor that lingered on the tongue.
etymology: From Latin 'sapor' (taste, flavor); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Food or nourishment; that which sustains.
exampleSentence: Bread and olives were the simple aliment of the mountain village.
etymology: From Latin 'alimentum' (nourishment), from 'alere' (to nourish); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rich Spanish stew of meats and vegetables; any miscellaneous mixture.
exampleSentence: The anthology was a delightful olla podrida of essays, poems, and recipes.
etymology: Spanish for 'rotten pot', 'olla' (pot) + 'podrida' (rotten); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sweet dessert of milk curdled with rennet.
exampleSentence: For pudding there was a wobbling junket dusted with nutmeg.
etymology: From Old French 'jonquette', from Latin 'juncus' (reed basket); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To soften a painting's colors or lines with a thin opaque, dry-brush layer.
exampleSentence: Turner would scumble pale clouds over a darker sky to evoke sea mist.
etymology: Probably a frequentative of 'scum' (to skim); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An opaque watercolor paint, or a painting made with it.
exampleSentence: She rendered the poster in flat, vivid fields of gouache.
etymology: French, from Italian 'guazzo' (watercolor); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small preliminary model for a sculpture or larger work.
exampleSentence: The sculptor shaped a clay maquette before casting the monument.
etymology: French, from Italian 'macchietta' (little sketch); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A design cut into a surface, the reverse of relief.
exampleSentence: The signet ring bore a tiny intaglio of a leaping stag.
etymology: Italian, from 'intagliare' (to engrave); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The green or bluish coating that forms on weathered copper or bronze.
exampleSentence: Centuries of rain had cloaked the statue in soft verdigris.
etymology: From Old French 'vert-de-Grece' (green of Greece); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An art technique of rubbing to transfer the texture of a surface.
exampleSentence: Max Ernst pioneered frottage, rubbing pencil over grained floorboards.
etymology: French, from 'frotter' (to rub); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A red mercury-sulfide mineral, source of the vermilion pigment.
exampleSentence: The lacquer box glowed a deep cinnabar red.
etymology: From Greek 'kinnabari', of Eastern origin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A white plaster ground prepared on a surface before painting.
exampleSentence: She brushed three coats of gesso onto the panel before sketching.
etymology: Italian, from Latin 'gypsum'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The bristling of body hair from cold, fear, or excitement; goose bumps.
exampleSentence: The choir's final chord sent a wave of horripilation down her arms.
etymology: From Late Latin 'horripilatio', from 'horrere' (to bristle) + 'pilus' (hair); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fleshy strip of tissue dividing the nostrils.
exampleSentence: The piercing passed neatly through her columella.
etymology: From Latin 'columella' (little column); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The small cartilage flap in front of the ear canal.
exampleSentence: He pressed the tragus to muffle the ringing in his ear.
etymology: From Greek 'tragos' (he-goat), for its tuft of hair; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The armpit.
exampleSentence: The nurse placed the thermometer in the patient's axilla.
etymology: From Latin 'axilla' (armpit); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small fold of tissue that restrains an organ's movement.
exampleSentence: The fold of skin beneath the tongue is the lingual frenulum.
etymology: From Latin 'frenulum' (little bridle); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Relating to the hollow at the back of the knee.
exampleSentence: The doctor checked the pulse in the popliteal artery behind his knee.
etymology: From Latin 'poples' (back of the knee); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fleshy mound of the palm at the base of the thumb.
exampleSentence: She massaged the aching thenar after a long day of typing.
etymology: From Greek 'thenar' (palm of the hand); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The eighth power of a number, in obsolete mathematical notation.
exampleSentence: In Recorde's notation, the zenzizenzizenzic of two is two hundred fifty-six.
etymology: Coined by Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in his 1557 'The Whetstone of Witte'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary, which holds only this single citation.
