definition: The slow apparent wobble of the moon seen from Earth.
exampleSentence: Thanks to libration, we can glimpse a little past the moon's near side.
etymology: From Latin 'libratio' (a balancing), from 'libra' (scales); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The point in an orbit nearest the sun.
exampleSentence: The comet blazed brightest as it swept through perihelion.
etymology: From Greek 'peri' (near) + 'helios' (sun); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The point in an orbit farthest from the sun.
exampleSentence: At aphelion the planet slows, drifting at its greatest distance from the sun.
etymology: From Greek 'apo' (away from) + 'helios' (sun); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A blossoming; also a powdery crystalline crust forming on a surface.
exampleSentence: A white efflorescence of salt bloomed across the damp brick wall.
etymology: From Latin 'efflorescere' (to blossom), from 'flos' (flower); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A point of greatest or least distance in an orbit.
exampleSentence: Each apsis marks where the satellite is nearest to or farthest from Earth.
etymology: From Greek 'hapsis' (arch, loop); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The property of a gel turning fluid when shaken and resetting at rest.
exampleSentence: The paint's thixotropy lets it flow under the brush yet not drip on the wall.
etymology: From Greek 'thixis' (touch) + 'trope' (turning); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The fully shadowed inner region of a shadow, as in an eclipse.
exampleSentence: Only within the moon's umbra does the sun vanish completely.
etymology: From Latin 'umbra' (shadow); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A table giving the calculated positions of a celestial body over time.
exampleSentence: The navigator consulted an ephemeris to fix the ship's position by the stars.
etymology: From Greek 'ephemeros' (lasting a day); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The unknowing fabrication of false memories without intent to deceive.
exampleSentence: His vivid account was pure confabulation, stitched from gaps in his memory.
etymology: From Latin 'confabulari' (to talk together); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A dissociative state of amnesia in which one wanders from home or identity.
exampleSentence: He emerged from the fugue days later in another city, with no memory of leaving.
etymology: From Latin 'fuga' (flight); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Channeling unacceptable impulses into socially constructive activity.
exampleSentence: Through sublimation he poured his restless anger into long-distance running.
etymology: From Latin 'sublimare' (to elevate); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The release of emotional tension by reliving a repressed experience.
exampleSentence: The session triggered a sudden abreaction, and years of grief poured out.
etymology: From Latin 'ab-' (away) + 'reaction', translating German 'Abreagieren'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Love of strangers; warm, generous hospitality toward guests.
exampleSentence: The villagers' philoxenia meant no traveler ever went unfed.
etymology: From Greek 'philos' (loving) + 'xenos' (stranger); a headword in Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A code of silence and refusal to cooperate with authorities.
exampleSentence: The whole neighborhood maintained an unbreakable omerta about the crime.
etymology: Sicilian Italian 'omerta', perhaps from Spanish 'hombredad' (manliness); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The belief in a shared humanity binding all people: 'I am because we are'.
exampleSentence: Her leadership was rooted in ubuntu, treating every worker as part of one family.
etymology: From Nguni Bantu 'ubuntu' (humanity); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Cozy, convivial, and pleasantly sociable.
exampleSentence: The candlelit cafe felt wonderfully gezellig on a rainy night.
etymology: Dutch, from 'gezel' (companion); a documented loanword in English-language media, listed in the Cambridge Dutch-English Dictionary.

definition: The science and art of measuring time and making timepieces.
exampleSentence: His passion for horology filled the shelves with antique clocks.
etymology: From Greek 'hora' (hour) + '-logia' (study); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to a leap year or its extra day.
exampleSentence: February gains a day in every bissextile year.
etymology: From Latin 'bisextilis', from 'bis' (twice) + 'sextus' (sixth); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Weekly; occurring once every seven days.
exampleSentence: The society held its hebdomadal meeting every Thursday evening.
etymology: From Greek 'hebdomas' (seven, a week), from 'hepta' (seven); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Mist or fog, especially the cold haze that gathers in winter or at the foot of hills.
exampleSentence: By dawn a soft brume had settled over the valley, blurring the hedgerows into ghosts.
etymology: Borrowed from French brume, from Latin bruma, a contraction of brevissima dies, 'the shortest day' — so the word literally carries midwinter inside it. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Twilight; the soft half-light of dusk.
exampleSentence: In the gloam the garden lost its colours one by one until only the white roses remained.
etymology: A poetic back-formation related to the more common 'gloaming', from Old English glōm, 'twilight'. Merriam-Webster labels it archaic. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The beginning of evening; the falling of dusk.
exampleSentence: At evenfall the swallows came low over the water, stitching the last light to the dark.
etymology: A gentle Old English compound of 'even' (evening) and 'fall', recorded for centuries in pastoral verse. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Evening twilight; the hour at dusk.
exampleSentence: They walked home at cockshut, when the last rooks were folding into the elms.
etymology: From the time of day when poultry are shut in to roost; first recorded in 1592 and used by Shakespeare in Richard III ('Much about cockshut time, from troop to troop'). Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The dim light of dusk or early evening, when owls begin to stir.
exampleSentence: We lingered in the owl-light until the hills became one shadow and the first call drifted across the field.
etymology: A charming compound of 'owl' and 'light', recorded since the 1500s for the half-light favoured by owls. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The first light of day; the dawn, often with a sense of new beginning.
exampleSentence: At the dayspring the frost on the meadow flared pink, and the whole field seemed to draw breath.
etymology: A 14th-century compound meaning the 'springing up' of day, made famous by its appearance in the Gospel of Luke. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The forming of dew, and the hour of evening when it begins to settle.
exampleSentence: By dewfall the grass had turned silver and cold, and our footprints darkened behind us.
etymology: A quiet English compound of 'dew' and 'fall', recorded since the 19th century for both the moisture and the moment. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The glow that lingers in the sky after sunset; also the warm feeling that remains after a happy experience.
exampleSentence: Long after the others had gone to bed she sat in the afterglow of the day, unwilling to let it end.
etymology: A 19th-century compound of 'after' and 'glow' that drifted naturally from the sky into the heart. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A rainbow formed by moonlight rather than sun, faint and often ghostly pale.
exampleSentence: Above the waterfall a moonbow hung in the spray, so faint we doubted our own eyes.
etymology: A modern compound of 'moon' and 'bow', describing a phenomenon noted as far back as Aristotle. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The eerie phosphorescent glow given off by certain fungi on rotting wood.
exampleSentence: Deep in the wood the fallen logs gave off a faint foxfire, a cold green light with no flame at all.
etymology: Possibly from Old French fois ('false'), so 'false fire'; an old country name for the glow of luminous fungi. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Fine filmy cobweb seen floating in calm air; anything exquisitely light and delicate.
exampleSentence: Threads of gossamer drifted across the lane, catching the low sun like spun glass.
etymology: From Middle English 'goose summer' — the mild late-autumn spell when such webs appear, perhaps because the silk resembled goose down. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: (Of wind) blowing strongly with a roaring sound; (of a place) exposed to such wind.
exampleSentence: The farmhouse stood on a wuthering ridge where the wind never quite stopped its low complaint.
etymology: A Yorkshire dialect word from Old Norse hvitha, 'a squall of wind', made immortal by Emily Brontë's Wuthering Heights. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The vault of the heavens; the sky regarded as a great arching expanse.
exampleSentence: Out where no town lights reached, the whole firmament blazed at once and we forgot to speak.
etymology: From Latin firmamentum, 'a support', via the Vulgate's rendering of the sky as a solid dome. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The highest reaches of heaven; the realm of pure light and fire.
exampleSentence: From the summit the dawn seemed to open straight into the empyrean, gold upon endless gold.
etymology: From Greek empyros, 'fiery', the ancients' name for the heaven of pure flame beyond the stars; used by Milton and Dante. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Deep sky-blue; the clear blue of a cloudless heaven or calm sea.
exampleSentence: The lake lay perfectly cerulean, a single colour from shore to shore.
etymology: From Latin caeruleus, 'dark blue', related to caelum, 'sky' — so the colour is named for heaven itself. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A swelling, rounded mass of cumulus cloud rising before a thunderstorm.
exampleSentence: A thunderhead stacked itself over the plain all afternoon, white at the top and bruised below.
etymology: A vivid American compound of 'thunder' and 'head', for the towering head of a storm cloud. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sky dappled with rows of small white clouds resembling the markings on a mackerel's back.
exampleSentence: A mackerel sky spread overhead at evening, ribbed and silver, promising a change in the weather.
etymology: A sailors' and shepherds' phrase, recorded for centuries in the rhyme 'mackerel sky, never long wet, never long dry'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fertile, low-lying coastal grassland of the Scottish and Irish west, famous for its summer carpet of wildflowers.
exampleSentence: In June the machair erupts into a riot of orchids and clover above the white sand.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic machair, 'fertile plain'; one of the rarest habitats in Europe, found only on the windward Atlantic shores. Listed in Collins.

definition: A small rocky island or reef, often awash at high tide.
exampleSentence: Seals hauled out on the skerry at low water, grey humps on the black rock.
etymology: From Old Norse sker via the Scots of Orkney and Shetland, where such rocks fringe every coast. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small bay or narrow sea inlet, as found in Orkney and Shetland.
exampleSentence: The boat slipped into the still voe, where the only sound was water lapping on shingle.
etymology: From Old Norse vágr, 'bay'; a Northern Isles word for the long fingers of sea that reach into the land. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A waterfall, or the deep pool at its foot; also a steep ravine.
exampleSentence: We followed the burn until it tumbled white over the linn into a pool black with peat.
etymology: A Scots word, recorded from 1513, blending Scottish Gaelic linne ('pool') with Old English hlynn ('torrent'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A sudden rise or rush of a stream from heavy rain or melting snow; a small freshwater rivulet.
exampleSentence: The spring freshet came down off the mountain overnight and turned the quiet brook into a roar.
etymology: From 'fresh' plus the diminutive -et; in use since the 1500s for the swelling of streams in thaw. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A sudden flood in a river; by extension, a rush or outpouring of anything.
exampleSentence: After three days of rain the river was in spate, brown and muscular between its banks.
etymology: A word of Scots and northern English origin, of uncertain root, long used for rivers running high. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A circular movement of water, air or mist running contrary to the main current.
exampleSentence: Leaves spun in a slow eddy at the river's edge, going nowhere, content to circle.
etymology: Probably from Old Norse iða, 'whirlpool'; in English since the 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small stream or trickling brook.
exampleSentence: A thread-thin rill ran down the hillside, singing to itself among the stones.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps from Low German or Dutch ril; a favourite of poets from Milton onward. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A tiny stream or rivulet; a little channel of running water.
exampleSentence: Rain gathered into a runnel along the gutter and carried a fleet of petals away.
etymology: An alteration of the older 'rinel', from Old English rynel, a diminutive of 'run'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A brook or mountain stream, especially one with a stony bed (Northern English).
exampleSentence: The children spent the whole afternoon damming the beck with pebbles and shrieking at the cold.
etymology: From Old Norse bekkr, 'brook'; the ordinary word for a stream across much of northern England. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small steep-banked mountain lake or pool.
exampleSentence: High above the valley a black tarn lay perfectly still, mirroring a sky it would never reach.
etymology: From Old Norse tjǫrn, 'small mountain lake'; a word native to the fells of northern England. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A lake, pool or broad expanse of standing water (poetic and dialectal).
exampleSentence: Mist hung low over the mere at dawn, so that the reeds seemed to grow out of cloud.
etymology: From Old English mere, 'sea, lake'; the OED marks the lake sense as poetical or dialectal. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A small, deep, wooded valley or dell.
exampleSentence: Bluebells flooded the dingle so thickly that the floor of the wood looked like spilled sky.
etymology: From Middle English meaning 'a deep hollow', perhaps akin to Old English dung. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A short, deep valley running into a hillside, often dry at the head.
exampleSentence: They followed the lane into a quiet combe where sheep grazed and the wind could not reach.
etymology: From Old English cumb, ultimately of Celtic origin; common in West Country place names. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A steep, bowl-shaped hollow at the head of a valley, carved by ice.
exampleSentence: Snow lingered in the high cwm long after the lower slopes had turned to green.
etymology: Borrowed directly from Welsh cwm, 'valley'; one of the few English words with no vowel letter. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A rounded hollow scooped into a mountainside by a former glacier.
exampleSentence: We ate our lunch in the shelter of the corrie, ringed by cliffs and the cries of ravens.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic coire, 'cauldron'; the Highland name for these natural mountain amphitheatres. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A steep, narrow ravine or wooded gorge, usually with a stream running through it.
exampleSentence: The path dropped into a shadowed clough where ferns dripped and the beck rang on the rocks.
etymology: From Old English clōh; a dialect word of the Pennines for a wooded cleft in the hills. Listed in Collins.

definition: A narrow, secluded valley, especially among mountains.
exampleSentence: Smoke rose straight from a single chimney far down the glen, the only sign of anyone at all.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic and Irish gleann, 'valley'; carried into English from the Celtic north and west. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A valley, especially a wide and gentle one (chiefly poetic).
exampleSentence: Below them lay a green vale threaded by a river, almost too peaceful to be real.
etymology: From Old French val, from Latin vallis, 'valley'; long beloved of poets for its softness of sound. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: An open meadow or grassland, especially one used for grazing.
exampleSentence: At dusk the cattle moved slowly across the lea, dark shapes against the failing gold.
etymology: From Old English lēah, 'open ground, clearing'; one of the oldest words in the English landscape. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A tract of open, rolling upland or down.
exampleSentence: The road ran for miles across the bare wold, with nothing between us and the sky.
etymology: From Old English weald, 'forest, high open land'; the same root as 'weald'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A high, barren hill or stretch of moorland (Northern English).
exampleSentence: They climbed the fell in a clinging mist and broke through, suddenly, into clean cold sunlight.
etymology: From Old Norse fjall, 'mountain'; the everyday word for the high ground of Cumbria and the north. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A hillside or the steep bank of a river or valley (Scots).
exampleSentence: She ran down the brae with her arms wide, the wind taking her laughter up the glen.
etymology: From Old Norse brá, 'eyelash, brow', via Scots, where it names every slope in the land. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A high, weathered outcrop of rock crowning a hill, especially on moorland.
exampleSentence: The granite tor stood against the sky like the ruin of some forgotten tower.
etymology: From Old English torr, of Celtic origin; characteristic of Dartmoor and the West Country. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small wood or wooded hill (archaic and poetic).
exampleSentence: At the edge of the holt a single deer lifted its head, then was gone among the trees.
etymology: From Old English holt, 'wood'; Merriam-Webster and Collins mark this sense archaic or poetic. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A small wood or thicket, especially one planted to shelter game.
exampleSentence: A blackcap was singing somewhere in the little spinney behind the barn.
etymology: From Old French espinei, 'a thorny place', from Latin spina, 'thorn'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A pleasant shady recess in a garden or wood, sheltered by leaves and boughs.
exampleSentence: They found a green bower of hazel where the light fell in coins and no one could see them.
etymology: From Old English būr, 'dwelling, chamber'; later the leafy retreat of pastoral poetry. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A light, springing rhythm in music or speech; a gentle rise and fall.
exampleSentence: There was a lilt in her voice when she spoke of home that she never seemed to notice.
etymology: From Middle English lilten, of obscure origin, first used of merry singing. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A low, continuous humming or vibrating sound.
exampleSentence: All night the thrum of rain on the tin roof held us somewhere between sleep and waking.
etymology: Imitative in origin, echoing the sound it names; in English since the 16th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To make a bubbling, gurgling sound, as flowing water does.
exampleSentence: The stream burbled over its stones in the dark, a sound so steady it felt like company.
etymology: Imitative, formed in Middle English to mimic the noise of bubbling water. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To sing with trills and quavering, sweet notes, as a bird does.
exampleSentence: A blackbird warbled from the topmost twig as though daring the morning to stay grey.
etymology: From Old French werbler, 'to sing with trills', of Germanic origin. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A temporary calm or quiet, especially a pause in a storm or in activity.
exampleSentence: In the lull between songs you could hear the sea, patient and enormous, beyond the open door.
etymology: Imitative, from the soothing sounds used to quiet a child to sleep (compare 'lullaby'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The slow, solemn sound of a bell, especially one rung for a death or ending.
exampleSentence: The single knell carried over the rooftops, and for a moment the whole town seemed to pause.
etymology: From Old English cnyllan, 'to strike a bell'; long associated with mourning. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A slow, mournful song or lament for the dead.
exampleSentence: The wind in the chimney kept up its low dirge while the house slept on around it.
etymology: From Latin dirige, 'direct', the first word of a Latin funeral antiphon. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To wail in grief; to lament loudly for the dead in the Irish tradition.
exampleSentence: The women keened at the graveside, a sound older than any words could be.
etymology: From Irish caoinim, 'I weep'; the keening of mourners is an ancient funeral rite. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fragrant essential oil distilled from flowers, especially rose petals.
exampleSentence: One drop of attar of roses filled the whole room, summoning a summer years gone by.
etymology: From Persian and Arabic ʿitr, 'perfume, essence'; the costliest of rose distillations. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A gentle current of scent, sound or air drifting by.
exampleSentence: A waft of woodsmoke reached her on the path, and at once she was eight years old again.
etymology: From the verb 'waft', probably from Dutch or Low German wachten, 'to guard, escort'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Something fragrant and soothing; anything that heals, comforts or eases pain.
exampleSentence: After the noise of the city, the silence of the hills was pure balm.
etymology: From Latin balsamum, 'aromatic resin'; the soothing of the body became the soothing of the soul. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fit of low spirits or sulky gloom; a vague, causeless melancholy.
exampleSentence: A grey Sunday always gives me the mulligrubs, that low gloom with no real cause behind it.
etymology: A fanciful 16th-century coinage, perhaps from 'megrim'; once also meant a stomach gripe. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A fit of low spirits or depression; also a passing whim or fancy.
exampleSentence: He shut the curtains, took to his chair, and gave himself up to the megrims for the afternoon.
etymology: An old form of 'migraine', from Greek hēmikrania, 'half the skull'; the headache became a mood and a caprice. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A weary listlessness and dissatisfaction born of boredom and a sense of life's emptiness.
exampleSentence: By the third week of rain a great ennui had settled over the house, heavier than any task.
etymology: From French ennui, from Latin in odio, 'in hatred'; long naturalised in English. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A pleasant or dreamy weariness; a soft, heavy lack of energy.
exampleSentence: A warm languor stole over them on the riverbank, and no one could be bothered to row home.
etymology: From Latin languere, 'to be faint or weak'; in English the word softened into something almost luxurious. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of weary listlessness; physical or mental fatigue and lack of will.
exampleSentence: A heavy lassitude held her to the bed, as though the air itself had grown too thick to move through.
etymology: From Latin lassus, 'weary'; the noun of pure tiredness. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Too great or extreme to be expressed in words.
exampleSentence: Standing at the canyon's edge, she felt an ineffable awe.
etymology: From Latin 'ineffabilis' — 'in-' (not) + 'effari' (to utter).

definition: A spell of low spirits, listlessness or stagnation; a period when nothing seems to move.
exampleSentence: January found him in the doldrums, the holidays gone and spring still impossibly far off.
etymology: From 'dull', influenced by 'tantrum'; later the name for the calm equatorial belt where sailing ships stalled. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Restlessness or uneasiness of mind; a quiet, nagging disquiet.
exampleSentence: A faint inquietude kept her at the window long after midnight, watching a road where no one came.
etymology: From Latin inquietudo, 'unrest', from in- ('not') plus quietus ('calm'). Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Tearfully or weakly sentimental, often after drink or in self-pity.
exampleSentence: Two glasses of wine and he turned maudlin, dredging up every old sorrow he could find.
etymology: From the name Mary Magdalene, often depicted weeping; her name softened into a word for tears. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Tearful; given to weeping, or tending to bring tears.
exampleSentence: The film was so relentlessly lachrymose that by the end the whole row was sniffling into their sleeves.
etymology: From Latin lacrima, 'tear'; a word that almost weeps as you say it. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Expressing or sounding a wistful sorrow; mournful in a soft, appealing way.
exampleSentence: A plaintive whistle came from the marsh, the loneliest sound she had ever heard.
etymology: From Old French plaintif, from plainte, 'lament'; the same root as 'complain'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Feeling or showing gentle, wry regret or sorrow.
exampleSentence: She gave a rueful smile at the photograph, half-amused, half-mournful at who they used to be.
etymology: From Old English hrēow, 'sorrow, repentance'; the same root as 'rue', the herb of regret. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To feel or express discontent; to fret or pine in low spirits.
exampleSentence: There was no use to repine over the lost letters; she packed them away and turned to the window.
etymology: Formed from 're-' plus 'pine', 'to languish with longing'; in use since the 1500s. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To be overcome with rapture or emotion, almost to the point of fainting.
exampleSentence: The first warm evening of the year, with lilac on the air, was enough to make anyone swoon.
etymology: From Old English geswōgen, 'in a faint'; later the word for being undone by feeling. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Hopelessly infatuated; so smitten as to lose all sense.
exampleSentence: He was utterly besotted, walking into lampposts because he could not stop reading her letters.
etymology: From 'be-' plus 'sot', 'fool'; literally to be made foolish, here by love. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Pining from unrequited or lost love; forsaken by the one you love.
exampleSentence: He wandered the lovelorn weeks of autumn writing letters he would never send.
etymology: From 'love' plus 'lorn', an old past participle of 'leese', 'to lose'; literally 'lost in love'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Looking sorrowful, dejected or in a sorry state.
exampleSentence: He sat on the kerb, woebegone, clutching the ticket for the train he had just missed.
etymology: From Middle English wo begon, 'beset with woe'; the woe has, quite literally, gone all over you. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Grieved or sorrowful at heart; aching with sadness.
exampleSentence: She left the old house heartsore, looking back once at the window of her childhood room.
etymology: A plain, old English compound of 'heart' and 'sore'; the soreness is grief itself. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Full of sadness; melancholy and pensive.
exampleSentence: There was something tristful in the way the light left the room, slow and reluctant as a goodbye.
etymology: From Latin tristis, 'sad', via Old French; a quieter cousin of 'sad' that English has nearly forgotten. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: So unhappy that nothing can console or comfort you.
exampleSentence: The dog lay disconsolate by the door for days after the boy went away to school.
etymology: From Latin disconsolatus, 'without solace', from consolari, 'to comfort'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Deprived of something or someone dear, and left desolate by the loss.
exampleSentence: With the last guest gone and the lights off, the house felt suddenly bereft.
etymology: The old past participle of 'bereave', from Old English berēafian, 'to rob, deprive'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Dejected and dispirited, with one's pride or hopes suddenly cast down.
exampleSentence: He came back from the audition crestfallen, his sheet music still rolled tight in his fist.
etymology: From the drooping crest of a defeated cockerel; the metaphor dates from the 1500s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A faint or desperate hope that is very unlikely to be fulfilled.
exampleSentence: He kept the porch light burning every night, a forlorn hope that she might still find her way back.
etymology: A mishearing of Dutch verloren hoop, 'lost troop' — once a band of soldiers sent on a doomed first assault, now a hope against hope. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Deep, sincere sorrow and remorse for having done wrong.
exampleSentence: His contrition was real; you could see it in the way he could not meet anyone's eyes.
etymology: From Latin contritus, 'worn down, crushed'; sorrow that grinds the heart small. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Engaged in deep, dreamy and often slightly sad thought.
exampleSentence: She grew pensive at the station, watching the rails run together toward a place she would not go.
etymology: From Old French pensif, from penser, 'to think', from Latin pensare, 'to weigh'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Full of gentle, yearning sadness; longing for something lost or unattainable.
exampleSentence: He gave a wistful glance at the children playing, remembering when summers had no end.
etymology: Probably from the older 'wistly', 'intently', blended with 'wishful'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Giving or showing joy; cheerful and full of gladness.
exampleSentence: A gladsome noise of children spilled out of the schoolyard and filled the whole grey street.
etymology: From Old English glæd, 'glad', plus '-some'; a word that has kept its old warmth. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Cheerful, merry and lighthearted.
exampleSentence: She set off down the lane in a blithesome mood, swinging her basket and humming to no one.
etymology: From Old English blīthe, 'happy, kindly', plus '-some'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Nimble and graceful; also cheerful and free from care.
exampleSentence: With the exams behind her she felt suddenly lightsome, as if she might float up the stairs.
etymology: From 'light' plus '-some'; meaning both 'full of light' and 'light of heart'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Cheerful and lighthearted; sprightly with good humour.
exampleSentence: The whole company grew jocund as the fire took hold and the songs began.
etymology: From Latin jucundus, 'pleasant', influenced by jocus, 'joke'; used by Wordsworth of his dancing daffodils. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Overflowing with excitement, enthusiasm and high spirits.
exampleSentence: She was ebullient after the good news, unable to sit still or stop talking for an hour.
etymology: From Latin ebullire, 'to boil over'; high spirits literally bubbling up. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Full of eager anticipation and excitement.
exampleSentence: The children were agog at the window, breath fogging the glass, waiting for the first snow.
etymology: Probably from Old French en gogues, 'in merriment'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of awed astonishment and curious delight.
exampleSentence: She gazed up into the cathedral's vaulting in pure wonderment, her argument quite forgotten.
etymology: From 'wonder' plus '-ment'; in English since the 16th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Extravagantly enthusiastic or ecstatic; overflowing with joyful feeling.
exampleSentence: He went rhapsodic about the little harbour town, as if no one had ever seen the sea before.
etymology: From Greek rhapsōidia, the recitation of epic poetry; later any flight of ardent feeling. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A state of supreme blessedness, serene and complete happiness.
exampleSentence: For one whole afternoon, with the baby asleep on her chest, she knew a kind of beatitude.
etymology: From Latin beatus, 'blessed, happy'; the same root as the Beatitudes of the Gospels. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Calmness and composure, especially under strain; an even, untroubled mind.
exampleSentence: She bore the long delay with an equanimity the rest of us could only envy.
etymology: From Latin aequus animus, 'even mind'; the balance of a steady spirit. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Delight and enjoyment; the pleasure taken in something agreeable.
exampleSentence: He laid out the cheeses and the wine with evident delectation, rubbing his hands together.
etymology: From Latin delectatio, 'a delighting', from delectare, 'to charm'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A deep, cosy contentment created by simple comforts, warmth and good company.
exampleSentence: Candles lit, wool socks on, the storm shut outside and the kettle singing — that is hygge.
etymology: A Danish untranslatable, from a Norwegian word for 'wellbeing'; Collins named it a Word of the Year in 2016. A foreign untranslatable from Danish. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Odds and ends; assorted small objects or bits and pieces, often of little value.
exampleSentence: He emptied his pockets onto the table: keys, string, a conker, and all the usual gubbins.
etymology: From the old word 'gobbon', 'a fragment'; Merriam-Webster labels it British dialect. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A fanciful ornament or contrivance; a trinket, knick-knack or whim.
exampleSentence: The mantelpiece was crowded with whigmaleeries — tiny brass animals, a glass dome, a clock that never told the truth.
etymology: A playful 18th-century Scots word of unknown origin; Merriam-Webster and Collins both mark it chiefly Scottish. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Something full of twists and turns; fanciful, excessively intricate detail.
exampleSentence: The old map was a crinkum-crankum of lanes and footpaths that led, as far as we could tell, nowhere.
etymology: A reduplication of 'crank', 'a bend or twist'; first recorded in the 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A confused jumble or hotchpotch of unrelated things.
exampleSentence: Her desk was a gallimaufry of receipts, seashells and half-finished poems.
etymology: From 16th-century French galimafrée, a stew thrown together from odd scraps of meat. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A confused mixture or hodgepodge, especially of ideas or nonsense.
exampleSentence: The pamphlet was a farrago of rumour, half-truth and pure invention, and he believed every word.
etymology: From Latin farrago, 'mixed fodder for cattle', from far, 'grain'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A noisy and overexcited reaction; a hubbub or fuss.
exampleSentence: There was a tremendous brouhaha at the gate, all of it over a goat that had escaped its pen.
etymology: From French brouhaha, probably imitative of confused noise. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A commotion or fuss, especially one caused by disagreement.
exampleSentence: There was a great kerfuffle over the seating plan, and in the end nobody sat where they were told.
etymology: From Scots curfuffle, from Gaelic car, 'to twist', plus fuffle, 'to dishevel'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A brief but deeply unpleasant or embarrassing experience.
exampleSentence: Waiting outside the head teacher's office, he lived through a genuine mauvais quart d'heure.
etymology: A French phrase, literally 'bad quarter of an hour', naturalised into English. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A small, beautiful trinket or curio prized for its charm and prettiness rather than any use.
exampleSentence: On her windowsill sat a row of bibelots - a glass swan, a thimble, a tiny brass key - each one a memory she couldn't bear to throw away.
etymology: A fanciful French formation on bel ('beautiful'); the OED's earliest English evidence is from 1873. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Tenderness and compassion for another's suffering - the very feeling whose absence we name in 'ruthless'.
exampleSentence: Watching the stray shiver in the rain, she felt a sudden ruth that sent her out with a towel and a bowl of warm milk.
etymology: From Middle English ruthe, from ruen ('to rue, feel sorrow'); first known use in the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The state of having quietly fallen into disuse; the still, dusty hush of something no longer used.
exampleSentence: The old ballroom had drifted into desuetude, its chandeliers furred with dust and its piano silent for decades.
etymology: From Latin desuescere ('to become unaccustomed'), from suescere ('to become accustomed'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Softly whispering or rustling, like leaves or hushed voices.
exampleSentence: The susurrant wind through the poplars sounded almost like the sea, and she stood still just to hear it.
etymology: From Latin susurrare ('to whisper, murmur'), from susurrus ('a whisper'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Sweetly soothing to the ear; gently and pleasingly melodious.
exampleSentence: She fell asleep to the dulcet tones of her grandmother's lullaby, the words half-lost but the sweetness intact.
etymology: From Middle English doucet, via Anglo-French from Latin dulcis ('sweet'), in use since the 1400s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Unfading and everlasting, like the mythical flower that never dies; also of a deep purplish-red.
exampleSentence: He liked to imagine their friendship as something amaranthine - a thing that would outlast every season and every quarrel.
etymology: From amaranth (a legendary unwithering flower), from Greek amarantos ('unfading'); the OED's earliest evidence is from 1667, in Milton. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A strong, restless longing to travel and roam, to be anywhere but here.
exampleSentence: Every autumn the wanderlust returned, and she would find herself pricing flights to cities she had never seen.
etymology: From German, literally 'desire to wander', from wandern ('to wander') + Lust ('desire'); first used in English around 1902. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To make one's slow, meandering way somewhere, in no particular hurry.
exampleSentence: They wended home through the back lanes, stopping to watch the swifts and to let the evening cool around them.
etymology: From Old English wendan ('to turn'), causative of windan ('to wind'); it is also the source of the past tense 'went'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of a soft, dusty, sea-glass colour between grey, blue and green; or coated with a delicate powdery bloom.
exampleSentence: The glaucous leaves of the eucalyptus seemed to hold the morning mist in their pale, waxy haze.
etymology: From Latin glaucus, from Greek glaukos ('gleaming, grey'); first recorded as a colour word in English in 1671. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep, luminous blue-green - the colour of pine shadows and deep summer foliage.
exampleSentence: At dusk the forest turned a single shade of viridian, as though someone had dipped the whole valley in cool green ink.
etymology: From Latin viridis ('green'); the pigment was first prepared in Paris in 1838 and first used as a colour name in English in the 1860s. Listed in Collins.

definition: Vanishing almost as soon as it appears; fleeting and fragile, like mist or a held breath.
exampleSentence: Happiness, he decided, was evanescent by nature - best caught in glimpses rather than chased.
etymology: From Latin evanescere ('to fade away, vanish'), also the source of 'vanish'; in English since the early 1700s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Pleasantly wooded and shady, thick with bushes and small trees.
exampleSentence: They picnicked in a bosky corner of the park where the light fell green and dappled through the leaves.
etymology: From bosk ('a thicket'), a Middle English variant of 'bush'; the adjective dates to the early 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of the woods; belonging to or evoking the quiet beauty of a forest.
exampleSentence: The cottage stood in a sylvan hush, ringed by oaks so old they seemed to be listening.
etymology: From Latin Silvanus, god of the woods, from silva ('forest'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Richly melodious and pleasant-sounding, like birdsong or a full-throated choir.
exampleSentence: The blackbird's canorous evening song poured down from the chimney pot like something rehearsed.
etymology: From Latin canorus, from canere ('to sing'); first used in English in 1646. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Giving cool, welcome shade; pleasantly shadowed by leaves.
exampleSentence: On the hottest afternoons the whole street drifted to the umbrageous bench beneath the plane tree.
etymology: From Latin umbra ('shade, shadow'), via French ombrageux; in English since 1587. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Perfectly clear and untroubled, with the soft transparency of pure water.
exampleSentence: The pool was so limpid that the pebbles on the bottom seemed close enough to touch.
etymology: From Latin limpidus ('clear'); in English since the early 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Bubbling with irrepressible high spirits; fizzy with life and delight.
exampleSentence: She had an effervescent way of greeting people that made even a rainy Monday feel like the start of something.
etymology: From Latin effervescere ('to boil up'), from fervere ('to be hot'); in English since the late 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Filled with a low, continuous, soothing murmur, like a stream or a distant crowd.
exampleSentence: The murmurous hum of the summer garden - bees, leaves, far-off voices - lulled him into a half-sleep.
etymology: From murmur (ultimately an imitative root shared with Sanskrit murmurah, 'crackling fire'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or belonging to summer; having the warm, drowsy character of summertime.
exampleSentence: There was an estival heaviness to the afternoon, the kind that makes clocks feel optional.
etymology: From Latin aestivalis, from aestas ('summer'); also spelled 'aestival'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Full of woods and groves; densely and beautifully forested.
exampleSentence: Beyond the meadow lay a nemorous slope where the light never quite reached the forest floor.
etymology: From Latin nemorosus, from nemus ('grove, wood'). Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Golden in colour or brilliance; gilded with warm, glowing light.
exampleSentence: The late sun laid an aureate sheen across the wheat, and for a moment the whole field looked minted.
etymology: From Late Latin aureatus ('decorated with gold'), from Latin aurum ('gold'); in English from the early 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Dazzlingly bright; shining with a radiant, resplendent light.
exampleSentence: The fireworks left a fulgent ghost on the dark, a brightness the eye kept seeing after the sky went black.
etymology: From Latin fulgere ('to shine brightly'); in late Middle English. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Tinged with the soft pink of a rose, especially the blush of dawn or dusk.
exampleSentence: They watched the roseate light spread across the snowfields until the whole valley seemed to blush.
etymology: From Latin roseus, from rosa ('rose'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The gentle, lapping sound of light splashing water.
exampleSentence: The only sound on the lake was the soft plash of the oars and the drip between strokes.
etymology: Probably imitative, from Late Old English plaesc ('pool, puddle'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Lush with fresh green growth; richly and vividly leafy.
exampleSentence: After the rains the hills turned verdurous almost overnight, green to the very edge of the sky.
etymology: From verdure (ultimately Latin viridis, 'green') + -ous; in English from around 1600. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A vivid calling-to-mind of the past; the act of remembrance itself.
exampleSentence: The smell of woodsmoke triggered a sudden anamnesis - she was eight again, and her father was raking leaves.
etymology: From Greek anamnesis ('remembrance'), from ana- ('back') + mimneskein ('to call to mind'); in English from the 1650s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Mother-of-pearl: the iridescent inner lining of certain shells, shifting through rainbow lights.
exampleSentence: She turned the shell in her palm and the nacre flushed pink, then green, then a watery silver.
etymology: Via Medieval Latin from Old Italian naccara, ultimately from Arabic naqqarah; in English from the 1590s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Heavy with sleepiness; drowsy, or inducing a warm and pleasant drowsiness.
exampleSentence: The somnolent afternoon, thick with heat and the drone of bees, made reading impossible and dozing inevitable.
etymology: From Latin somnolentus, from somnus ('sleep'); in English from the late 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to the evening; having the quiet, falling quality of dusk.
exampleSentence: A vesperal calm settled over the harbour as the last boats turned for home.
etymology: From Late Latin vesperalis, from vesper ('evening'); in English from around 1620. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Silvery and bright; shining with the pale gleam of polished silver.
exampleSentence: The moon laid an argent path across the water, straight as a road to the horizon.
etymology: From Latin argentum ('silver, money'), via Anglo-French; in late Middle English. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Blissful and heavenly; belonging to a state of perfect, serene happiness.
exampleSentence: For one elysian week the rain held off, the figs ripened, and nobody had anywhere they needed to be.
etymology: From Latin Elysium, from Greek Elysion, the mythical paradise of the blessed dead. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Heavenly and lofty; seeming to come from a higher, more luminous world.
exampleSentence: There was a supernal stillness to the cathedral at dawn, as if the air itself were holding its breath.
etymology: From Medieval Latin supernalis, from Latin supernus ('that is above'), from super ('above'); in English from the 1470s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Icy cold; chilled to a clear, glassy, almost beautiful coldness.
exampleSentence: She dipped her hand into the gelid mountain stream and pulled it back, laughing at the shock of it.
etymology: From Latin gelidus ('icy cold'), from gelu ('frost'); in English from around 1600. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Something held sacred - a holy place, relic, or sanctuary that one would swear by.
exampleSentence: He kept his mother's ring as a kind of private halidom, a small holy thing in a world that held little sacred.
etymology: From Old English haligdom, from halig ('holy') + -dom; attested before the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Deep and serene happiness; a state of being blessedly, contentedly glad.
exampleSentence: There was a quiet felicity in the ordinary evening - warm bread, an open book, the dog asleep at her feet.
etymology: From Latin felicitas ('happiness'), from felix ('happy, fortunate'); in late Middle English. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A state of calm, restful peace - the deep ease of being at rest in body and mind.
exampleSentence: In sleep his face lost its worry entirely, settling into a repose she hadn't seen in years.
etymology: From Old French reposer, from Late Latin repausare ('to cause to rest'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Warm, infectious gladness expressed in laughter and good cheer.
exampleSentence: The kitchen rang with mirth as the children tried, and failed, to flip the pancakes.
etymology: From Old English myrgth, from myrge ('pleasant, merry'); attested before the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Intense warmth of feeling; burning passion, eagerness, or zeal.
exampleSentence: She threw herself into the campaign with an ardor that swept the more cautious volunteers along with her.
etymology: From Latin ardor ('a flame, burning'), from ardere ('to burn'); in late Middle English. Also spelled 'ardour'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sharp, persistent craving or longing for something.
exampleSentence: All winter she had a yen for the sea - not a holiday, exactly, just the smell of salt and the sound of gulls.
etymology: From Chinese (Cantonese) yan ('a craving'), originally an opium craving; in English from the early 20th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The state of being utterly captivated or held spellbound by someone or something.
exampleSentence: The whole hall sat in thrall to the old storyteller, afraid that a single cough might break the spell.
etymology: From Old Norse thraell ('a slave, bondman'); attested before the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Trembling, quivering - often with emotion, tenderness, or fragile hope.
exampleSentence: She gave a tremulous smile, somewhere between laughter and tears, and reached for his hand.
etymology: From Latin tremulus ('trembling'), from tremere ('to tremble'); in English from the early 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A low, unsettled feeling of unease; quiet anxiety with no clear cause.
exampleSentence: A vague disquiet followed her all day, as if she'd forgotten something important she couldn't name.
etymology: From dis- ('opposite of') + quiet, modelled on French desquieter; in English from the 1500s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Restless and impatient; fidgeting against confinement or delay.
exampleSentence: The audience grew restive as the interval stretched on, shifting and murmuring in their seats.
etymology: From Old French restif ('motionless, stubborn'), from rester ('to remain'); the sense shifted from balking to fidgeting. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A soaring, buoyant joy; the lightness of spirits lifted high.
exampleSentence: When the letter said yes, a wave of elation carried her around the room before she'd even finished reading.
etymology: From Latin elatus ('raised, lifted up'), past participle of efferre ('to carry out, raise'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A state of delighted wonder, as though under a beautiful spell.
exampleSentence: The first snowfall held the children in pure enchantment, faces pressed to the glass at the falling white.
etymology: From Old French enchantement, from Latin incantare ('to sing a spell upon'), from cantare ('to sing'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Shimmering with rainbow colours that shift and change with the light.
exampleSentence: A film of oil on the puddle turned iridescent, a small accidental rainbow at the side of the road.
etymology: From Latin iris ('rainbow'), from Greek; coined in English in the late 18th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Softly gleaming with a deep, lovely sheen.
exampleSentence: Her hair was lustrous in the lamplight, catching the glow like dark water.
etymology: From Latin lustrare ('to brighten, illuminate'), related to lux ('light'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Marked with soft, shifting patches of light and shade.
exampleSentence: They walked the dappled path beneath the beeches, sunlight and shadow sliding over their shoulders.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to Old Norse depill ('a spot'); popularised by Gerard Manley Hopkins's 'dappled things'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Vividly green and flourishing with fresh vegetation.
exampleSentence: After a week of rain the meadow was impossibly verdant, almost glowing under the grey sky.
etymology: From Old French verd ('green'), from Latin viridis. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or like the spring; fresh, youthful and newly green.
exampleSentence: There was a vernal energy in the office that Monday, as if everyone had decided at once to begin again.
etymology: From Latin vernalis, from ver ('spring'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or belonging to winter; having winter's cold, still character.
exampleSentence: A hibernal hush lay over the village, every chimney smoking and every door shut against the cold.
etymology: From Latin hibernalis, from hibernus ('wintry'); in English from the 1620s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Mild and merciful, especially of weather that is gentle and forgiving.
exampleSentence: The forecast promised a clement afternoon, so they risked a picnic without coats.
etymology: From Latin clemens ('mild, merciful'); in English from the 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An open, sunlit clearing in the heart of a wood.
exampleSentence: They stumbled into a glade where the light fell straight down and a single deer stood watching.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, perhaps related to 'glad' in an old sense of 'bright, shining'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A small, secluded, often wooded valley.
exampleSentence: In the dell behind the house, sheltered from the wind, the first bluebells always came early.
etymology: From Old English dell, related to 'dale'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A broad, open valley, especially among hills.
exampleSentence: From the ridge they could see the whole dale spread below, stitched with stone walls and grazing sheep.
etymology: From Old English dael ('valley'), shared with Old Norse dalr. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Low, flat, watery marshland - a quiet country of reeds and mist.
exampleSentence: Fog hung low over the fen at dawn, and the only movement was a heron lifting from the reeds.
etymology: From Old English fenn ('mud, mire, marsh'); attested before the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A stretch of wooded or once-wooded open country.
exampleSentence: The road wound through the weald, past oak woods and hop fields and villages that hadn't changed in centuries.
etymology: From Old English weald ('forest, wooded upland'); related to German Wald. Listed in Collins.

definition: A small stream; a thin, running thread of water.
exampleSentence: A rivulet of meltwater traced its way down the path, bright and busy in the spring sun.
etymology: From Italian rivoletto, diminutive of rivo ('stream'), from Latin rivus. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A great rolling wave, or a swelling surge of cloud, smoke, or fabric.
exampleSentence: A billow of white curtain bellied out of the open window, then sank slowly back against the sill.
etymology: From Old Norse bylgja ('a wave'); in English from the 1550s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Foam or froth, especially the white spray flung up by the sea.
exampleSentence: Spume blew off the breakers in long white streaks and salted their faces where they stood on the pier.
etymology: From Latin spuma ('foam'); in late Middle English. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Salt water; the sea, with all its cold, briny tang.
exampleSentence: The whole town smelled of brine and diesel and frying fish, and she loved every bit of it.
etymology: From Old English bryne; attested before the 12th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The luminous, shifting curtains of light in the polar sky; also, the radiance of dawn.
exampleSentence: They lay back in the snow as the aurora rippled overhead in slow green folds, too astonished to speak.
etymology: From Latin aurora ('dawn'), also the Roman goddess of the dawn. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A faint, wavering light; or a small, hopeful trace of something.
exampleSentence: Far across the moor a single glimmer told them the inn was still awake and waiting.
etymology: From Middle English glimeren, of Germanic origin, related to 'gleam'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To dawdle and dally; to spend time idly and pleasantly doing nothing in particular.
exampleSentence: Stop lollygagging by the window and help me carry these in before it rains!
etymology: American English, of uncertain origin, first recorded in the 1860s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To waste time by loitering or being unable to make up one's mind.
exampleSentence: We dillydallied over the menu so long that the kitchen nearly closed before we ordered.
etymology: A playful reduplication of 'dally', from Middle English dalien ('to chat, trifle'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To pamper and overprotect, treating someone with excessive tenderness.
exampleSentence: His grandmother loved to mollycoddle him, pressing second helpings on him and tucking blankets he didn't need.
etymology: From 'Molly' (a pet form of Mary, used for an effeminate man) + 'coddle'; in English from the 19th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To cuddle and caress affectionately; to kiss and embrace fondly.
exampleSentence: The young couple canoodled on the park bench, oblivious to the pigeons and the passing world.
etymology: American English of uncertain origin, first recorded in the mid-19th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To utterly bewilder or confuse; to leave someone at a baffled loss.
exampleSentence: The riddle flummoxed the whole table, and we finally gave up and begged for the answer.
etymology: English dialectal, probably imitative; first recorded around 1837 and used by Dickens. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To throw into comic confusion; to disconcert and fluster.
exampleSentence: The sudden round of applause discombobulated him so thoroughly that he forgot his own name.
etymology: A playful, mock-Latin American coinage of the 1830s, probably altering 'discompose'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To run away hurriedly; to make a quick, scrambling exit.
exampleSentence: The moment the bell rang, the whole class skedaddled for the door and the summer beyond it.
etymology: American English, of uncertain origin, popularised during the Civil War in the 1860s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A great noisy commotion or fuss; a cheerful uproar.
exampleSentence: There was such a hullabaloo when the team scored that the neighbours came out to see what had happened.
etymology: Probably a rhyming reduplication of the dialect word 'hullo'; in English from the 1760s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Foolish, exaggerated talk; insincere nonsense.
exampleSentence: He waved away the salesman's malarkey about miracle cures and walked straight back out of the shop.
etymology: American English of unknown origin, first recorded in the 1920s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Senseless, pompous nonsense; meaningless talk dressed up as wisdom.
exampleSentence: 'Pure balderdash,' the professor snorted, tossing the pamphlet of predictions into the bin.
etymology: Origin uncertain; in the 1590s it meant a jumbled mixture of drinks before coming to mean nonsense. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Empty, ridiculous nonsense.
exampleSentence: The idea that cats can't be trained is, in my experience, complete poppycock.
etymology: From Dutch dialect pappekak ('soft dung'); brought to American English in the 19th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Trifling fuss and nonsense; showy but useless trivialities.
exampleSentence: She wanted a plain, quiet wedding, with none of the folderol of doves and ten-tier cakes.
etymology: From a meaningless refrain ('fol-de-rol') once sung in old songs; in this sense from the 1820s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A long, rambling, pointlessly complicated procedure or account.
exampleSentence: Getting the parcel released from customs turned into an afternoon-long rigmarole of forms and queues.
etymology: An 18th-century alteration of 'ragman roll', a long medieval list of names. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Playfully fanciful humour; a charming, slightly absurd turn of imagination.
exampleSentence: The garden was full of whimsy - a teapot fountain, a door to nowhere, gnomes reading tiny newspapers.
etymology: Probably from 'whim-wham', a fanciful trifle; in English from the 1600s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To leap and prance about in high-spirited, exuberant play.
exampleSentence: The lambs cavorted across the field, springing sideways for the sheer joy of having legs.
etymology: American English of uncertain origin, perhaps an alteration of 'curvet'; from around 1794. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A silly, foolish person - said more with affection than malice.
exampleSentence: 'You absolute nincompoop,' she laughed, 'you've put your jumper on inside out again.'
etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in the 1670s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A mischievous rascal or scamp, roguish but somehow likeable.
exampleSentence: The little rapscallion had eaten half the cake and blamed it, with great sincerity, on the dog.
etymology: An alteration of the older 'rascallion', from 'rascal'; in English from the 1690s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A ragged, dishevelled child or person of charmingly untidy appearance.
exampleSentence: The puppy came home a muddy ragamuffin, trailing leaves and looking thoroughly pleased with itself.
etymology: From Middle English Ragamuffin, the name of a demon in Langland's 'Piers Plowman' (14th century). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A young, cheeky, overconfident person who presumes above their years.
exampleSentence: 'When I was your age,' grumbled the old man, 'a whippersnapper like you wouldn't dare answer back.'
etymology: A 17th-century compound, probably from 'whip snapper' (an idle person who cracks whips). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Fussily precise about small details; hard to please.
exampleSentence: He was persnickety about his coffee - exactly ninety-four degrees, exactly one sugar, in exactly that mug.
etymology: An altered form of the Scots word 'pernickety', of uncertain origin; in English from the 1880s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Bad-tempered, argumentative, and difficult to get along with.
exampleSentence: The cantankerous old tomcat tolerated exactly one person and hissed at everyone else.
etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps blending 'contentious' and 'rancorous'; from the 1770s. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Irritable and full of odd, contrary whims; grumpily set in one's ways.
exampleSentence: By the third sleepless night the whole household had grown crotchety and short with one another.
etymology: From 'crotchet' ('a perverse whim, an odd notion'), from Old French crochet ('a little hook'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A lover, especially a secret or forbidden one.
exampleSentence: The diary, found a century later, was addressed entirely to a paramour history had never named.
etymology: From Old French par amour ('by love, with love'); used as a noun in English from the 14th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A young rustic lover or suitor; a country sweetheart.
exampleSentence: In the old ballad the shepherdess turns away every swain but one, and weeps for him in the end.
etymology: From Old Norse sveinn ('a boy, servant, attendant'); the romantic sense developed in pastoral poetry. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A woman who flirts playfully and charmingly, without serious intent.
exampleSentence: She played the coquette at the ball, dazzling a dozen partners and promising her heart to none of them.
etymology: From French coquette, feminine of coquet ('a flirtatious person'), from coq ('cock, rooster'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An innocent, artless young woman; the wide-eyed naive role in a play or film.
exampleSentence: She arrived in the city a true ingenue, astonished by everything, suspicious of nothing.
etymology: From French ingenue, feminine of ingenu ('ingenuous, innocent'), from Latin ingenuus. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A person or thing without equal; the unmatched best of its kind.
exampleSentence: As a maker of violins he was a nonpareil, and collectors crossed oceans to hold his work.
etymology: From French nonpareil ('without equal'), from non- ('not') + pareil ('equal'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A model of supreme excellence; a perfect example of some quality.
exampleSentence: She was held up as a paragon of patience, though privately she admitted to counting to ten quite often.
etymology: From Old Italian paragone ('a touchstone for testing gold'), via French. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Lasting only a very short time; here and gone, like a mayfly or a mood.
exampleSentence: The cherry blossom is loved precisely because it is ephemeral, gone within a week of arriving.
etymology: From Greek ephemeros ('lasting only a day'), from epi ('on') + hemera ('day'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Former; belonging to a time that is now past.
exampleSentence: Her erstwhile rival became, years later, her closest and most trusted friend.
etymology: From erst ('earliest, formerly'), from Old English aerest, the superlative of aer ('before'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A temporary stay somewhere; a brief, often restful, dwelling away from home.
exampleSentence: Their sojourn by the lake was meant to last a weekend and stretched, happily, into a month.
etymology: From Old French sojorner, from Late Latin subdiurnare ('to spend the day'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sudden, illuminating moment of insight when everything falls into place.
exampleSentence: Halfway across the bridge she had an epiphany: she didn't have to go back at all.
etymology: From Greek epiphaneia ('a manifestation, appearance'), from epiphainein ('to show forth'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sudden, unpredictable change of mind or mood; a playful whim.
exampleSentence: On a caprice she got off three stops early and walked home the long way, through the market and the park.
etymology: From French caprice, from Italian capriccio ('a shiver, a sudden start'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An unpredictable, capricious turn of events, mind, or behaviour.
exampleSentence: They learned to plan around the vagaries of mountain weather, which could turn from sun to storm in an hour.
etymology: From Latin vagari ('to wander'), from vagus ('wandering'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A woman with whom one is deeply in love; one's beloved.
exampleSentence: He wrote to his inamorata every evening, sealing each letter as though it carried his whole heart across the sea.
etymology: From Italian innamorata, feminine of innamorato, from innamorare ('to inspire with love'), from amore ('love'). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Showy but trifling ornament or finery; pretty, frivolous, unnecessary stuff.
exampleSentence: Beneath all the frippery of ribbons and lace, it was, she realised, simply a very plain little hat.
etymology: From French friperie ('old clothes'), from Old French frepe ('a rag'); the ironic 'finery' sense dates to the 1630s. Listed in Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A showy but worthless little trinket; a flashy, useless ornament.
exampleSentence: The market stall glittered with gewgaws - plastic gems, tin rings, glass beads that lost their shine by morning.
etymology: From Middle English giuegaue, a reduplicated form of uncertain origin, attested around 1175. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A wistful awareness of the impermanence or transience of all things, and the gentle, bittersweet sadness at their passing.
exampleSentence: Watching the cherry petals drift onto the path, she felt a quiet mono no aware, tender and unhurried.
etymology: From Japanese, literally 'the pathos of things'; popularised by the 18th-century scholar Motoori Norinaga,  with the OED's earliest English evidence dating to 1940 in Monumenta Nipponica.  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A stirring feeling of emotional fervour, exuberance and joyful enthusiasm; a rousing of the spirit.
exampleSentence: By the last chorus the whole hall was singing with such hwyl that strangers had linked arms.
etymology: From Welsh, originally meaning a ship's sail  and hence one's 'course' or momentum in life; Collins glosses it as 'emotional fervour, as in the recitation of poetry' and tags it [C19: Welsh].  Listed in the Collins English Dictionary.

definition: A state of gentle, pervasive melancholy or sorrow.
exampleSentence: There was a faint tristesse to the empty seaside town in October.
etymology: From French tristesse, from Latin tristis 'sad'; in English since the 14th century.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Bright, glistening or lustrous; shining with a clear light.
exampleSentence: The rain left every leaf nitid in the low morning sun.
etymology: From Latin nitidus 'shining', from nitere 'to glisten';  in English from 1615.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A small wood, thicket or copse.
exampleSentence: They cut through the hazel shaw to reach the water meadow beyond.
etymology: From Old English sceaga 'thicket'; now archaic or dialectal.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Glowing or glittering with a reddish or golden light.
exampleSentence: The forge filled the barn with a rutilant glow that flickered on their faces.
etymology: From Latin rutilare 'to glow red', from rutilus 'ruddy'; in English from before 1460.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Wonderful, joyous, delightful.
exampleSentence: It was a frabjous afternoon: sunshine, old friends, and nowhere to be.
etymology: Coined by Lewis Carroll in 'Jabberwocky' (1871), probably blending 'fair', 'fabulous' and 'joyous'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A buoyant, wholehearted delight in being alive.
exampleSentence: Her joie de vivre was infectious; even queuing felt like an adventure with her.
etymology: From French, literally 'joy of living'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Peace of mind; tranquillity and freedom from anxiety.
exampleSentence: Only when the letter finally arrived did she find any heartsease.
etymology: From Middle English hertes ese 'ease of heart'  (used by Gower before 1393);  also a name for the wild pansy. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A sudden flash of intuitive enlightenment or awakening.
exampleSentence: Halfway up the mountain, breathless, he had a small satori about why he had come.
etymology: From Japanese satori 'awakening', a key term in Zen Buddhism. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The perfect, opportune moment for action; the decisive instant.
exampleSentence: He waited, sensing the kairos, and asked the question just as the room fell quiet.
etymology: From ancient Greek kairos 'the right moment', distinct from chronos (clock time). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Shining in the night; phosphorescent.
exampleSentence: The  wake of the boat turned noctilucous, every oar-stroke trailing cold fire.
etymology: From Latin nox, noct- 'night' + lucere 'to shine'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The faint light given off by the stars; starlight.
exampleSentence: There  was no moon, only starshine silvering the field.
etymology: From star + shine. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A growing warm; an increase of warmth or ardour.
exampleSentence: There was a slow incalescence between them over the long summer of letters.
etymology: From Latin incalescere 'to grow warm', from calere 'to be warm'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A halo or aureole; a ring of radiant light.
exampleSentence: The streetlamp gave the mist a faint gloriole, like a saint in a cheap icon.
etymology: From  French gloriole, from Latin gloriola, diminutive of gloria 'glory'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: St Elmo's fire: a glowing electrical discharge seen at the masthead or rigging of a ship in a storm.
exampleSentence: A blue corposant danced on the spar, and the old sailors crossed themselves.
etymology: From Portuguese corpo-santo, literally 'holy body'; Merriam-Webster gives a First Known Use of circa 1595,  while the OED's earliest evidence is from 1561 in Richard Eden's translation.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A pale light seen flickering over marshy ground at night; figuratively, a delusive hope.
exampleSentence: He chased the promotion like an ignis fatuus, always one bog further on.
etymology: Medieval Latin, literally 'foolish fire'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A flitting marsh-light that leads travellers astray; anything elusive that beckons and deceives.
exampleSentence: The perfect first sentence proved a will-o'-the-wisp that kept her up till dawn.
etymology: From 'Will (with the) wisp', a sprite imagined carrying a wisp of burning straw.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A wonder, a marvel; something strange and astonishing.
exampleSentence: The  frost had turned the whole orchard into a ferly of glass.
etymology: From Old English fǣrlic 'sudden, unexpected', from fǣr 'danger';  Scots and Northern English. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Full of yearning; longing and mournful.
exampleSentence: A  yearnful note in the old song made the whole table go quiet.
etymology: From yearn (Old English giernan 'to desire') + -ful. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Felt deeply within oneself; intimate, heartfelt, private.
exampleSentence: There  is a homefelt joy in a kitchen warm with the smell of bread.
etymology: From home + felt; used by Milton. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A lock of hair tangled as if by elves.
exampleSentence: She  came in from the wind laughing, all elflocks and bright cheeks.
etymology: From elf + lock; from a folk belief that elves matted sleepers' hair. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Glowing with light; luminous, or clear and translucent.
exampleSentence: The honey was lucent in the jar, holding the afternoon inside it.
etymology: From Latin lucent-, present participle of lucere 'to shine'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Reflecting light; shining back, gleaming.
exampleSentence: The lake lay relucent under the climbing moon.
etymology: From Latin relucere 'to shine back'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Shining brightly; lustrous, or illustrious.
exampleSentence: The beetle's back was splendent, a chip of green metal in the dust.
etymology: From Latin splendere 'to shine'; in English from the 15th century.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Glowing or dazzling, as if from great heat.
exampleSentence: The desert noon was candescent, the horizon trembling with white light.
etymology: From Latin candescere 'to grow white-hot', from candere 'to shine'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Glowing with heat; at white heat.
exampleSentence: The smith drew the candent iron from the coals.
etymology: From Latin candere 'to be shining white'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Dusky, sombre, drab; of a dull dark colour.
exampleSentence: The hall was subfusc and hushed, lit by a single high window.
etymology: From Latin subfuscus 'brownish, dusky', from fuscus 'dark'.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Shadowy, shaded; also secluded or retiring.
exampleSentence: He led an umbratile life among his books, untroubled by the world.
etymology: From Latin umbratilis, from umbra 'shade'.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Casting or giving shade; shady.
exampleSentence: They picnicked under the umbriferous limes by the river.
etymology: From Latin umbrifer 'shade-bringing', from umbra 'shade' + ferre 'to bear'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Cloudy or misty; figuratively, vague and obscure.
exampleSentence: The mountain kept a nubilous crown all morning.
etymology: From Latin nubilus 'cloudy', from nubes 'cloud'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Somewhat dark or dim; tending towards twilight.
exampleSentence: The duskish room smelled of woodsmoke and old paper.
etymology: From dusk + -ish. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Of or belonging to the dawn; of the early morning.
exampleSentence: An aurorean hush lay over the harbour before the gulls woke.
etymology: From Latin Aurora, goddess of dawn. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of the colour of flame; flame-like, fiery.
exampleSentence: The maples turned flammeous overnight, a whole street alight.
etymology: From Latin flammeus, from flamma 'flame'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The quality of being luminous or translucent; radiance, clearness.
exampleSentence: The water had a lucency you could read pebbles through.
etymology: From Latin lucent- 'shining' + -cy. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Sparkling; emitting sparks or flashes of light.
exampleSentence: Frost made the lawn scintillant in the first light.
etymology: From Latin scintillare 'to sparkle', from scintilla 'spark'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Flashing like lightning; brilliantly sudden.
exampleSentence: A fulgurant idea struck her mid-sentence and she stopped dead.
