etymology: From Latin fulgurare 'to flash, lighten', from fulgur 'lightning'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Glittering, sparkling.
exampleSentence: The river ran micant under the bridge lamps.
etymology: From Latin micare 'to glitter, quiver'; rare, recorded in the mid-17th century.  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Despair; a state of hopeless despondency.
exampleSentence: After the third refusal a kind of wanhope settled over him.
etymology: From Middle English wan- (a negative prefix) + hope. Listed in Collins.

definition: Something that banishes or eases grief; a comfort.
exampleSentence: Long  walks were her only dolorifuge that winter.
etymology: From Latin dolor 'grief' + -fuge 'driving away'; coined by Thomas Hardy in 'Tess of the d'Urbervilles' (1891) — 'a species of dolorifuge after the death of the horse'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To feel the lack of and long for; to wish for something missing.
exampleSentence: She  desiderated the quiet of her old house more than she would admit.
etymology: From Latin desiderare 'to long for'. Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Dreary and dismal; sad, low-spirited.
exampleSentence: It was a dowie, drizzling sort of day that suited his mood exactly.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, of uncertain origin; recorded from the early 16th century.  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Muddy or turbid; cloudy; also gloomy and troubled.
exampleSentence: The burn ran drumly after the storm, brown with peat.
etymology: Scots, perhaps a variant of 'drubly'; recorded from before 1522.  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Gloomy and bleak; chilly; shivering with cold.
exampleSentence: He came in oorie and grey, glad of the fire.
etymology: Scots, recorded in the poems of Robert Burns (1787).  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: To waste away with longing or suffering; to pine utterly.
exampleSentence: She would not forpine for a man who never wrote.
etymology: From the intensive prefix for- + pine. Listed in Collins.

definition: Woe, sorrow, grief.
exampleSentence: Her face was a picture of wae as the train pulled out.
etymology: Scots form of English 'woe'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Grief, affliction, or trouble (archaic).
exampleSentence: He bore his teen in silence, telling no one of the loss.
etymology: From Old English tēona 'injury, grief'. Listed in Collins.

definition: Hidden, secret; also dreary or sorrowful.
exampleSentence: They  met in some dern corner of the garden where no one walked.
etymology: From Old English dyrne 'secret, hidden'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Sad, sorrowful, melancholy.
exampleSentence: There was something triste about the shuttered cafe in the rain.
etymology: From French triste, from Latin tristis 'sad'.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Dreary, bleak and wet; dismal and tediously long.
exampleSentence: It was a dreich Tuesday, the kind that never quite gets light.
etymology: Scots, from Old Norse drjúgr 'lasting, enduring'. Listed in Collins.

definition: Keen and biting; of weather or wind, bitterly cold.
exampleSentence: A snell wind came off the firth and cut straight through them.
etymology: From Old English snel 'quick, active'; Scots and Northern English.  Listed in Collins.

definition: A bright vermilion or scarlet colour; also, gilded silver.
exampleSentence: At sunset the whole estuary turned to vermeil and beaten gold.
etymology: From Old French vermeil, from Latin vermiculus 'little worm' (the source of crimson dye). Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A wet sea-mist or haze drifting in from the coast.
exampleSentence: A cold fret rolled off the North Sea and swallowed the pier.
etymology: English regional (chiefly eastern coast) in the 'sea fret' sense. Listed in Collins.

definition: A foolish or gawky person; also a cuckoo.
exampleSentence: Standing  there like a gowk, he forgot every word of his speech.
etymology: From Old Norse gaukr 'cuckoo'; Scots and Northern English. Listed in Collins.

definition: To know; to be aware of (archaic).
exampleSentence: Little did she weet what the morning would bring.
etymology: From Old English witan 'to know'. Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The blended chirping or murmur of many birds; a din of voices.
exampleSentence: At dusk the hedge was loud with the chirm of roosting sparrows.
etymology: From Old English cirm 'an outcry, noise'.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A low, vibrant, whirring or trilling sound, as of certain birds or insects.
exampleSentence: The nightjar's churr rose and fell across the heath.
etymology: Of imitative origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: To nestle or cuddle close together for warmth; also to coo softly.
exampleSentence: The  children croodled under one blanket while the storm passed.
etymology: Scots and dialectal, from 'crood' 'to coo'; recorded from before 1810.  Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A low, deep murmur or roar.
exampleSentence: You  could feel the brool of the waterfall before you could see it.
etymology: Of imitative or uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: Of a horse, to whinny or neigh softly; to nicker.
exampleSentence: The  mare whickered as soon as she heard the gate.
etymology: Of imitative origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: To tangle or entangle; (as a noun) a muddle or snarl.
exampleSentence: The  kitten had fankled the whole ball of wool round the chair legs.
etymology: Scots, from 'fank' 'a coil or noose'. Listed in Collins.

definition: A commotion, fuss or row.
exampleSentence: There  was a fair stooshie at the meeting over the new car park.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: A great fuss over a trifle; also showy, frivolous finery.
exampleSentence: All  that foofaraw over a misplaced comma!
etymology: American, of uncertain origin, perhaps from Spanish fanfarrón 'braggart'; mid-19th century.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A lively, wrangling dispute or quarrel.
exampleSentence: After much argy-bargy they finally agreed where to eat.
etymology: A reduplication of dialectal 'argy' (a variant of argue); mid-19th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Dust, or a swirling cloud of dust; also turmoil.
exampleSentence: The threshing raised a golden stoor that hung in the barn light.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from Old French estour 'armed combat'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: To hesitate or be undecided; to dither.
exampleSentence: She  swithered on the doorstep, key in hand, then turned back.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: A muddle or mess; (as a verb) to grope for fish with the hands.
exampleSentence: The spare room was in a complete guddle by the end of the move.
etymology: Scots, probably imitative; recorded from the early 19th century.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Of or belonging to the present day; of today.
exampleSentence: He kept a careful record of every hodiernal joy, however small.
etymology: From Latin hodiernus, from hodie 'today'; recorded from 1656.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Late in occurring, developing or flowering; of the late season.
exampleSentence: The  serotine roses bloomed on into the frosts.
etymology: From Latin serotinus 'late', from sero 'late'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The time of evening; eventide.
exampleSentence: At  vespertide the bells began across the valley.
etymology: From Latin vesper 'evening' + tide 'time'. Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Keenness of perception or insight; discernment.
exampleSentence: Her percipience caught the lie behind his easy smile.
etymology: From Latin percipere 'to perceive'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A low, often moist or marshy hollow in the land.
exampleSentence: Mist pooled in the swale long after the hill had cleared.
etymology: Perhaps from Old Norse svalr 'cool', or a Middle English word for a shady spot.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: An emerald; an old name for a green gem.
exampleSentence: The  sea over the reef was the deep green of a smaragd.
etymology: From Latin smaragdus, from Greek smaragdos; in English from before 1300.  Listed in Merriam-Webster, Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Magic, enchantment; occult learning.
exampleSentence: The  forest had an air of gramarye, as if the trees were listening.
etymology: From Old French gramaire 'learning, book of magic', related to 'grammar' and 'glamour'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Otherworldly and elfin; whimsically strange; also, fated to die.
exampleSentence: There was something fey about the child, as if she heard music no one else did.
etymology: From Old English fǣge 'doomed to die'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: To bask in the sun; to soak up sunlight.
exampleSentence: The  cat apricated on the windowsill all afternoon.
etymology: From Latin apricari 'to bask', from apricus 'sunny'. Listed in Collins.

definition: A roofed gateway to a churchyard, once a resting place for the coffin before burial.
exampleSentence: They stood under the lichgate while the rain hammered the yews.
etymology: From Old English līc 'corpse, body' + gate; recorded from the 1480s. Listed in Collins and the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A girl or young woman (East Anglian dialect).
exampleSentence: She'd  been a bright mauther, always first across the harvest field.
etymology: East Anglian dialect, of uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: A small bunch of flowers; also, an old word for a short motto inscribed in a ring.
exampleSentence: He  left a posy of violets on the doorstep without a note.
etymology: A contraction of 'poesy'; recorded from the 15th century.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Fullness; abundance; the state of being complete and replete.
exampleSentence: There was a plenitude to those long childhood summers that nothing since has matched.
etymology: From Latin plenus 'full' + -tude.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A freckle.
exampleSentence: A  summer of haymaking had scattered ferntickles across her nose.
etymology: Scots and Northern dialect, linking 'fern' (its seed-like speckles) with 'tickle/speckle'. Listed in Collins.

definition: To smooth over or explain away with fair words; to flatter.
exampleSentence: He  tried to gloze the disaster as 'a learning experience'.
etymology: From Old French gloser 'to comment, interpret', related to 'gloss'.  Listed in Collins.

definition: A conciliatory gift or gratuity; also, sweetness of manner.
exampleSentence: A small douceur to the doorman worked wonders.
etymology: From French douceur 'sweetness', from Latin dulcis 'sweet'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: Tender feeling; fondness and affection.
exampleSentence: He spoke of his old teacher with real tendresse.
etymology: From French tendresse, from tendre 'tender'.  Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Graciousness and nobility of conduct; courtesy and good breeding.
exampleSentence: He treated the waiter with a gentilesse that told you everything about him.
etymology: From Old French gentilesse, from gentil 'noble'; used by Chaucer. Listed in Collins and Merriam-Webster.

definition: Softness; gentleness or luxurious ease (now rare).
exampleSentence: The whole room invited mollitude: deep chairs, low lamps, a slow fire.
etymology: From Latin mollitudo, from mollis 'soft';  recorded from 1599.  Listed in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: Neat, trim and tidy; smooth.
exampleSentence: She kept a snod little cottage with not a thing out of place.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, of uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: Lively, brisk and cheerful; in good spirits.
exampleSentence: For  ninety, she was as canty as a woman half her age.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from 'cant' 'lively'. Listed in Collins.

definition: Calm, still and sheltered; quiet.
exampleSentence: They found a lown spot out of the wind to eat their lunch.
etymology: From Old Norse logn 'calm'; Scots.  Listed in Collins.

definition: Dizziness; a swimming of the head.
exampleSentence: The fairground waltzer left the children with the mirligoes.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain, probably imitative origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: Growing red; reddening, blushing.
exampleSentence: His rubescent ears gave away how much the praise meant to him.
etymology: From Latin rubescere 'to grow red', from ruber 'red'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Becoming green; greenish.
exampleSentence: By late March the hedges were virescent again, just barely.
etymology: From Latin virescere 'to grow green', from virere 'to be green'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Becoming white; growing pale or whitish.
exampleSentence: The albescent sky just before snow has a particular hush to it.
etymology: From Latin albescere 'to grow white', from albus 'white'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A state of stillness, calm and tranquillity.
exampleSentence: She had found a deep quietude in the months of solitary walking.
etymology: From Latin quietus 'at rest'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The full moon; the time of the full moon.
exampleSentence: Under the plenilune the whole orchard stood in silver.
etymology: From Latin plenilunium, from plenus 'full' + luna 'moon'. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An unexpected, often unwelcome sequel to something thought finished.
exampleSentence: Just when the scandal seemed over, an afterclap arrived in the morning post.
etymology: From after + clap (a sudden blow); recorded from the 15th century. Listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To endure or bear patiently; to put up with.
exampleSentence: She had tholed worse winters than this and said so.
etymology: From Old English tholian 'to suffer, endure'; Scots and Northern English. Listed in Collins.

definition: Spirited, resourceful energy; mettle and common sense.
exampleSentence: It took real smeddum to start again from nothing at her age.
etymology: Scots, from Old English smedema 'fine flour, the finest part'. Listed in Collins.

definition: Drenched, soaked to the skin.
exampleSentence: They arrived drookit and laughing, leaving puddles in the hall.
etymology: Scots, of uncertain origin. Listed in Collins.

definition: Shy, bashful and diffident.
exampleSentence: He was too blate to ask her to dance, and regretted it for years.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, perhaps from Old English blāt 'pale, wan'. Listed in Collins.

definition: The lingering ringing or jingling of bells.
exampleSentence: The whole valley filled with the tintinnabulation of the morning bells.
etymology: From Latin tintinnabulum 'bell'; popularized by Edgar Allan Poe's poem 'The Bells' (1849).

definition: Occupying a threshold; in between two states or stages.
exampleSentence: Airports at 3 a.m. have a liminal feel — nowhere, between everywhere.
etymology: From Latin limen 'threshold'.

definition: Deep human flourishing; happiness as a whole life lived well.
exampleSentence: For Aristotle, pleasure was fleeting but eudaimonia was the point of a life.
etymology: From Greek eu 'good' + daimōn 'guiding spirit'; Aristotle's name for the highest human good.

definition: Unfamiliar and strange, yet marvellous.
exampleSentence: The first snow felt selcouth to the desert child — alien and wonderful at once.
etymology: From Old English seldcūth, from seldan 'seldom' + cūth 'known'.

definition: A surge of soul, passion, and authenticity in art or performance.
exampleSentence: Her voice cracked on the last note, and that was the duende — raw and alive.
etymology: Spanish duende 'goblin, spirit'; elevated by Federico García Lorca in a 1933 lecture to mean art's dark, vital magic.

definition: A wave-smashed chasm or fissure cut into a sea-cliff.
exampleSentence: The path skirted a zawn where the Atlantic boomed forty feet below.
etymology: Cornish dialect, from Cornish 'sawan' (chasm, gully); recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossary of landscape terms.

definition: A place where one feels safe, at home and from which one draws strength; one's deepest refuge.
exampleSentence: The old reading chair by the window was her querencia after a brutal week.
etymology: Spanish, from 'querer' (to want, to love) and ultimately Latin 'quaerere' (to seek); originally the part of the bullring a bull claims for its stand. Entered English via Hemingway's 'Death in the Afternoon' (1932).

definition: A person skilled in the art of dinner-table conversation; a brilliant talker over a meal.
exampleSentence: A natural deipnosophist, she could turn a dull supper into the night's best entertainment.
etymology: From Greek 'deipnon' (dinner) + 'sophistes' (master of a craft); from Athenaeus's c. 3rd-century work 'Deipnosophistai', in which learned men converse at a banquet.

definition: A habitual faultfinder who can sour any experience with discontent.
exampleSentence: Travel with a smelfungus and even the Alps will somehow be too cold, too steep and overrated.
etymology: Coined (as 'Smelfungus') by Laurence Sterne in 'A Sentimental Journey' (1768) to mock the relentlessly critical travel writer Tobias Smollett.

definition: A person who stubbornly clings to a habit or belief even after being shown it is wrong; also, the mistaken notion itself.
exampleSentence: He's a mumpsimus about the apostrophe and will defend his error to the grave.
etymology: From a tale of an illiterate priest who kept saying Latin 'mumpsimus' for 'sumpsimus' ('we have taken') and refused to be corrected; in English use since the 16th century.

definition: The anxious wakefulness in the small hours before dawn, when worries swell out of all proportion.
exampleSentence: At four in the morning, deep in uhtceare, every small problem felt like a catastrophe.
etymology: Old English, from 'uht(a)' (the restless hour before dawn) + 'cearu' (care, sorrow); found in Old English poetry such as 'The Wife's Lament'.

definition: A love of solitude and a longing to withdraw from other people.
exampleSentence: After the week-long conference, a wave of apanthropy sent her gladly home to silence.
etymology: 18th-century English, from Greek 'apo-' (away from) + 'anthropos' (human being).

definition: A wordless, charged look shared by two people who both want to begin something but each waits for the other to start.
exampleSentence: Across the table passed a long mamihlapinatapai before either dared to mention the kiss.
etymology: From the Yaghan language of Tierra del Fuego; the 1994 Guinness Book of World Records lists it as the 'most succinct word', glossed as looking at each other hoping the other will offer to do what both desire but neither will begin.

definition: The bowl-shaped hollow formed by cupping both hands together; a double handful.
exampleSentence: He scooped a gowpen of spring water and drank straight from his hands.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from Old Norse 'gaupn' (the cupped hands forming a hollow); attested in Older Scots from the late 15th century and in Merriam-Webster's unabridged dictionary.

definition: The whirring sound made by a covey of partridges bursting into flight.
exampleSentence: A sudden zwer from the stubble field marked where the birds had been hiding.
etymology: Exmoor dialect, an onomatopoeic term recorded in Robert Macfarlane's glossaries of nature words.

definition: A puppet on strings; figuratively, a politician whose actions are controlled by someone pulling the strings behind them.
exampleSentence: Voters grew tired of electing quockerwodgers who answered only to their donors.
etymology: 19th-century English; originally a wooden toy figure jerked by strings, later applied derisively to a politician acting at another's command.

definition: Having the soft, pearly iridescence of mother-of-pearl.
exampleSentence: At dawn the clouds turned nacreous, faintly pink and blue like the inside of a shell.
etymology: From 'nacre' (mother-of-pearl), via French from Italian 'nacchera', ultimately of Arabic origin, + the suffix '-ous'.

definition: Of or relating to yesterday or to a former time.
exampleSentence: He woke with a pridian headache, the lingering toll of the night before.
etymology: From Latin 'pridianus', from 'pridie' (on the day before).

definition: Having beautifully shaped buttocks.
exampleSentence: The sculptor was famed for his callipygian marble nymphs.
etymology: Dated to 1800; Latinised from Greek 'kallipygos' (the name of a statue of Aphrodite), from 'kalli-/kallos' (beauty) + 'pyge' (buttocks).

definition: Wandering alone; given to solitary roaming.
exampleSentence: She spent a solivagant summer crossing the hills with nothing but a pack and a map.
etymology: From Latin 'solus' (alone) + 'vagari' (to wander).

definition: Aiming at peace; conciliatory and inclined to smooth over conflict.
exampleSentence: Her irenic tone calmed the meeting just as it threatened to boil over.
etymology: From Greek 'eirenikos' (peaceful), from 'eirene' (peace).

definition: Of, relating to, or happening in the morning; active at dawn.
exampleSentence: His matutinal routine of coffee and birdsong was sacred and unhurried.
etymology: From Late Latin 'matutinalis', from Latin 'matutinus' (of the morning), linked to Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn.

definition: To give off flashing, glittering points of light; to sparkle.
exampleSentence: Frost made the whole meadow coruscate as the sun cleared the hedge.
etymology: From Latin 'coruscare' (to flash, glitter, vibrate).

definition: In a direction contrary to the sun's course; counterclockwise, traditionally regarded as unlucky.
exampleSentence: Folklore warned against walking widdershins around the old church.
etymology: From Middle Low German 'weddersinnes' (against the way), from 'wider' (against) + 'sin' (direction); naturalised into Scots and English.

definition: In the direction of the sun's apparent course; clockwise, traditionally regarded as auspicious.
exampleSentence: For luck, the bride was led deasil three times around the hearth.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic 'deiseil', related to 'deas' (right hand, south); the sunwise turn for good fortune.

definition: Early; in good time, before it is too late.
exampleSentence: We rose betimes to catch the tide while the harbour was still grey.
etymology: Middle English 'bitimes', from 'by' + 'time' + adverbial '-s'; in literary use since the 14th century.

definition: Perhaps; possibly; maybe.
exampleSentence: Aiblins he'll come round by spring, once the worst of his temper's cooled.
etymology: Scots, from 'able' + '-ins' (an adverbial suffix); literally 'ably', shading into 'possibly'. Familiar from the poems of Robert Burns.

definition: Freshly melted snow; very cold, half-thawed slush.
exampleSentence: The mountain stream ran with snowbroth, numbing his hands within seconds.
etymology: From Old English 'snāw' (snow) + 'broth'; in English from c.1600. Shakespeare uses it in 'Measure for Measure' (I.4), where Lucio calls Angelo 'a man whose blood is very snow-broth'.

definition: A person who begins to learn or study only late in life.
exampleSentence: A proud opsimath, he took up Greek and the cello in his seventies.
etymology: From Greek 'opse' (late) + 'manthanein' (to learn); in English from the 1650s.

definition: The worship of words.
exampleSentence: His epeolatry was incurable: he read the dictionary for pleasure and hoarded rare adjectives.
etymology: From Greek 'epos' (word) + '-latry' (worship); coined by Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. in 'The Professor at the Breakfast-Table' (Atlantic essays from 1859, collected as a book in 1860).

definition: Soft hail — the small white snow pellets formed when supercooled droplets freeze onto a falling snowflake.
exampleSentence: Graupel pattered against the tent like spilled rice before the real snow began.
etymology: From German 'Graupel', a diminutive of 'Graupe' (pearl barley, groats).

definition: A standing wave that sloshes slowly back and forth in an enclosed body of water such as a lake or harbour.
exampleSentence: After the earthquake a gentle seiche rocked the harbour for hours, lifting and dropping the moored boats.
etymology: Swiss French, of obscure origin; promoted as a scientific term by the hydrologist François-Alphonse Forel for the oscillations of Lake Geneva in 1890.

definition: The shrill chirping made by crickets and other insects rubbing body parts together.
exampleSentence: The summer dusk filled with the stridulation of a thousand crickets.
etymology: From French 'striduler', from Latin 'stridulus' (shrill, creaking), from 'stridere' (to creak).

definition: Greediness; an excessive, gluttonous appetite.
exampleSentence: He attacked the buffet with a gulosity that emptied three platters before the toast was finished.
etymology: From Late Latin 'gulositas', from Latin 'gulosus' (gluttonous), from 'gula' (throat, gullet); in English before 1500.

definition: Careless, illegible handwriting; a crude scrawl.
exampleSentence: The prescription was the usual medical griffonage, unreadable to everyone but the pharmacist.
etymology: From French 'griffonnage', from 'griffonner' (to scribble), ultimately from 'griffe' (claw).

definition: A person obsessively anxious about their own health, forever fearing illness.
exampleSentence: A lifelong valetudinarian, he travelled with a suitcase of remedies for ailments he did not have.
etymology: From Latin 'valetudinarius' (sickly), from 'valetudo' (state of health), from 'valere' (to be well); early 18th century.

definition: A neighbour whose house is on fire.
exampleSentence: Smoke pouring next door, he ran out shouting that he had become, of all things, a ucalegon's neighbour.
etymology: From Ucalegon, a Trojan elder whose house burned in the sack of the city (Virgil, 'Aeneid' 2.311–312, 'iam proximus ardet Ucalegon'); recorded as an English noun in Webster's New International Dictionary (1934).

definition: A noisy quarrel, brawl, or uproar.
exampleSentence: The council meeting collapsed into a full collieshangie over the parking scheme.
etymology: Scots, recorded from 1737; origin uncertain, perhaps from Gaelic 'coileid' (hubbub) or a fanciful compound of 'collie' (dog) and 'shangie'.

definition: Light, frivolous, teasing banter.
exampleSentence: Dinner was all persiflage and laughter, with nothing serious said for hours.
etymology: From French 'persiflage', from 'persifler' (to banter), from 'per-' (intensive) + 'siffler' (to whistle, hiss); mid-18th century.

definition: An informal chat; also a short, light, conversational essay or column.
exampleSentence: His Sunday causerie in the paper read like a friend talking to you over coffee.
etymology: From French 'causer' (to chat), from Latin 'causari'; the essay sense was popularised by Sainte-Beuve's 'Causeries du lundi' (1849).

definition: The ancient Greek virtue of moderation, self-control, and soundness of mind.
exampleSentence: Where others chased excess, she cultivated sophrosyne, wanting only enough.
etymology: From Greek 'sophrosyne', from 'sos' (sound, whole) + 'phren' (mind); a central virtue in Plato's 'Charmides' and in Aristotle.

definition: The metal cap or band fixed to the end of a tool handle, walking stick, or pencil to strengthen it.
exampleSentence: The rubber ferrule on his cane had worn away, and it clicked on the tiles with every step.
etymology: An alteration (influenced by Latin 'ferrum', iron) of Old French 'virol', from Latin 'viriola' (small bracelet), diminutive of 'viria' (bracelet).

definition: The small plastic or metal sheath at the end of a shoelace.
exampleSentence: The aglet had split, leaving the lace fraying and impossible to thread.
etymology: From Old French 'aiguillette', diminutive of 'aiguille' (needle), from Late Latin 'acucula', diminutive of Latin 'acus' (needle).

definition: The state of being only partly or carelessly dressed.
exampleSentence: She answered the unexpected knock in a state of deshabille, clutching her dressing gown shut.
etymology: From French 'déshabillé' (undressed), past participle of 'déshabiller' (to undress: 'dés-' un- + 'habiller' to dress); late 17th century.

definition: Dreamlike; of or relating to dreams.
exampleSentence: The film had an oneiric quality, its scenes dissolving into one another like half-remembered dreams.
etymology: From Greek 'oneiros' (dream); mid-19th century.

definition: Belonging to the drowsy, hallucinatory state just before falling asleep.
exampleSentence: In that hypnagogic drift she heard her name called, though the house was empty.
etymology: From French 'hypnagogique', from Greek 'hypnos' (sleep) + 'agogos' (leading, inducing); coined by Alfred Maury in the mid-19th century.

definition: Hungry; greedy or voracious.
exampleSentence: The esurient guests eyed the kitchen door long before dinner was announced.
etymology: From Latin 'esurire' (to be hungry), a desiderative of 'edere' (to eat); 17th century.

definition: Very fond of drinking alcohol; also, absorbent of liquid.
exampleSentence: After a bibulous evening at the inn, the poets staggered home reciting verse.
etymology: From Latin 'bibulus', from 'bibere' (to drink); 17th century.

definition: Seized by a violent, compulsive urge to write.
exampleSentence: Scripturient at midnight, she filled three notebooks before the fever passed.
etymology: From Late Latin 'scripturire' (to desire to write), a desiderative of Latin 'scribere' (to write); recorded in English from 1637.

definition: Caring little; nonchalant and indifferent.
exampleSentence: He met the bad news with a pococurante shrug, as though it concerned someone else entirely.
etymology: From Italian 'poco curante' (caring little); from the name of an indifferent Venetian senator in Voltaire's 'Candide' (1759).

definition: Of or relating to the day before yesterday.
exampleSentence: He could recall the nudiustertian dinner in perfect detail but not what he ate this morning.
etymology: From Latin 'nudius tertius', a contraction of 'nunc dies tertius est' (now is the third day); coined by Nathaniel Ward in 'The Simple Cobler of Aggawam' (1647).

definition: Of or belonging to yesterday.
exampleSentence: A faint hesternal sadness lingered, the residue of a quarrel the night before.
etymology: From Latin 'hesternus' (of yesterday) + English '-al'; in English from the late 18th century.

definition: To make a crackling or rattling sound, like a fire or dry leaves underfoot.
exampleSentence: The logs began to crepitate as the flames took hold.
etymology: From Latin 'crepitare' (to crackle), a frequentative of 'crepare' (to creak, crack); 1620s.

definition: To spend the summer in a dormant, torpid state — the hot-weather counterpart of hibernation.
exampleSentence: Buried in the cracked mud, the lungfish estivates until the rains return.
etymology: From Latin 'aestivare' (to spend the summer), from 'aestas' (summer).

definition: To laugh in a smothered, snorting way through the nose while trying to stifle it.
exampleSentence: The pupils snirtled behind their hands as the teacher's chalk snapped a third time.
etymology: Scots, a frequentative of 'snirt' (to snigger, snort); recorded from 1786 in the work of Robert Burns.

definition: To the very last drop; drunk down completely, leaving nothing behind.
exampleSentence: The vintage was so fine they drank it supernaculum, tipping the empty glasses to prove it.
etymology: A mock-Latin rendering of German 'auf den Nagel' (onto the nail), from the old custom of upturning the emptied glass on the thumbnail to prove it was drained; late 16th century.

definition: Of a dark, dusky brownish-grey colour.
exampleSentence: A fuscous moth settled on the windowsill.
etymology: From Latin 'fuscus' (dark, swarthy); first English use 1660s.

definition: The organic compound responsible for the earthy smell of soil and rain.
exampleSentence: That dark, earthy note after the storm is geosmin.
etymology: From Greek 'geo-' (earth) + 'osme' (smell). Coined in 1965 by biochemists Nancy N. Gerber and Hubert A. Lechevalier at Rutgers, isolating it from Streptomyces.

definition: A state of deep, gloomy absorption or reverie.
exampleSentence: He sat in a brown study, deaf to the conversation.
etymology: From 'brown' in the obsolete sense 'gloomy, dark' + 'study' in the obsolete sense 'reverie'; first attested 1532 (Dice-Play).

definition: A rich, heavy corded silk fabric, or a garment made of it.
exampleSentence: She wore a stiff gown of black paduasoy.
etymology: Alteration of French 'pou-de-soie', influenced by 'Padua say' (a serge from Padua, Italy). OED gives first English use 1663.

definition: A coarse woven woollen fabric or floor-cloth.
exampleSentence: A drugget protected the carpet beneath the dining table.
etymology: From French 'droguet', diminutive of 'drogue'; in English from the late 16th century.

definition: The part of a vocal or instrumental range in which most of a piece lies.
exampleSentence: The aria's high tessitura tires all but the strongest sopranos.
etymology: Italian 'tessitura' (texture, weaving), from 'tessere' (to weave); a doublet of 'texture'.

definition: A run of several notes sung on a single syllable.
exampleSentence: She ended the line on a soaring melisma.
etymology: From Greek 'melisma' (a song, tune), from 'melos' (song); in English from 1837.

definition: A rich, full outpouring of harmonious sound; the principal organ stop.
exampleSentence: The organ's diapason rolled through the nave.
etymology: From Greek 'dia pason (chordon)' (through all the notes); via Latin.

definition: Called; named; by the name of.
exampleSentence: A small inn yclept The Green Man stood at the crossroads.
etymology: Middle English, from Old English 'geclypod', past participle of 'clypian' (to call), with the perfective prefix 'y-'.

definition: A small slice or thick cut of meat, especially bacon.
exampleSentence: She fried a collop of bacon for breakfast.
etymology: Late Middle English 'collop', of North Germanic origin; compare Swedish 'kalops' (meat stew).

definition: A large knife; an old word for a knife-fight.
exampleSentence: He drew a wicked snickersnee from his belt.
etymology: Alteration of 'stick or snee', from Dutch 'steken' (to thrust) + 'snijden' (to cut); knife-fight sense 1690s.

definition: To make merry and drink healths; to carouse.
exampleSentence: Villagers wassailed through the orchard on Twelfth Night.
etymology: From Middle English 'wæs hæil', from Old Norse 'ves heill' (be in good health).

definition: Streaks of rain or snow that evaporate before reaching the ground.
exampleSentence: Grey virga trailed beneath the cloud but never wet the field.
etymology: From Latin 'virga' (rod, streak in the sky); meteorological sense from the mid-20th century.

definition: A faint, white arc seen in fog, like a colourless rainbow.
exampleSentence: A pale fogbow arched over the moor at dawn.
etymology: Blend of 'fog' + 'rainbow'; OED's earliest cite is 1820 (William Scoresby).

definition: Mist, fog or steam, especially sea fret rolling off the water.
exampleSentence: A cold roke crept up the estuary by evening.
etymology: Middle English 'roke' (fog, vapour), probably from Old Norse 'roka'; related to 'reek'.

definition: Shining at night; especially of high, tenuous clouds that glow after dusk.
exampleSentence: Noctilucent clouds shimmered silver-blue at midnight.
etymology: From Latin 'nox, noct-' (night) + 'lucent-' (shining), from 'lucere' (to shine); from 1812.

definition: A strong easterly wind of the western Mediterranean.
exampleSentence: A levanter funnelled through the strait, kicking up the swell.
etymology: From 'Levant' (the eastern Mediterranean), from French 'levant' (rising sun, east), from Latin 'levare' (to raise).

definition: An ornamental branched candle-holder, often backed by a mirror.
exampleSentence: A gilt girandole threw candlelight across the ballroom.
etymology: From French 'girandole', from Italian 'girandola', from 'girare' (to turn), from Late Latin 'gyrare'; c.1625–35.

definition: A 'living stone' — a squat succulent disguised as a pebble.
exampleSentence: Her windowsill lithops looked exactly like split grey stones.
etymology: From Greek 'lithos' (stone) + 'ops' (face, appearance); the genus was described from plants found in 1811 by William J. Burchell.

definition: An ancient water clock that measures time by flowing water.
exampleSentence: The orator's speech was timed by a clepsydra.
etymology: From Greek 'klepsydra', from 'kleptein' (to steal) + 'hydor' (water) — literally 'water thief'; in English from 1580.

definition: The branch of meteorology concerned with clouds.
exampleSentence: His nephology notebook named every cloud overhead.
etymology: From Greek 'nephos' (cloud) + '-logy' (study of).

definition: A stupor or trance; a sleeping draught; also deadly nightshade.
exampleSentence: He sank into a dwale and would not be roused.
etymology: Middle English 'dwale' (stupor, deception), from Old English 'dwala' (error), reinforced by Old Norse 'dvala' (sleep); used by Chaucer c.1390.

definition: Proud, splendid, fine or fair.
exampleSentence: The knight rode in armour wlonk and bright.
etymology: From Old English 'wlanc/wlonc' (stately, proud); found in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and Pearl.

definition: A soft murmuring, whispering or rustling sound.
exampleSentence: The susurration of the audience died as the lights dimmed.
etymology: From Latin 'susurrare' (to whisper), of imitative origin.

definition: To flirt or have casual love affairs with many people.
exampleSentence: He philandered shamelessly all summer.
etymology: From the obsolete noun 'philander' (a lover), from Greek 'philandros' (loving people/men).

definition: The giddy disorientation of being far from home in an unfamiliar country.
exampleSentence: The unfamiliar smells and signage filled her with a thrilling dépaysement.
etymology: French, from 'dé-' (un-) + 'pays' (country); the feeling of being 'un-countried', out of one's element.

definition: A frenzy of yearning for something impossible to attain.
exampleSentence: His nympholepsy for a vanished, idealized past kept him from ever living in the present.
etymology: From Greek 'nympholēptos', 'seized by nymphs'; the ancients believed such ecstasy struck those who glimpsed a nymph. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep-rooted sense of honour, dignity and duty toward family and community.
exampleSentence: Out of filotimo the old fisherman refused payment for ferrying the stranded family home.
etymology: Greek φιλότιμο, from 'philos' (love) + 'timi' (honour); literally 'love of honour', a cardinal Greek virtue.

definition: Giving confident opinions on matters well beyond one's actual knowledge.
exampleSentence: His ultracrepidarian lectures on medicine annoyed every doctor at the dinner.
etymology: From Latin 'ne ultra crepidam' ('not beyond the sandal'), the painter Apelles' rebuke to a meddling cobbler in Pliny; coined as an English word by William Hazlitt around 1819.

definition: Boldly self-confident, cheeky and a little flashily daring.
exampleSentence: The wee one strode onstage gallus as you like and belted the first note.
etymology: Scots, possibly from 'gallows' (one fit for the gallows, hence reckless); now an admiring word for swagger. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: Habitually gloomy, taciturn and darkly sardonic in temperament.
exampleSentence: He gave a saturnine half-smile and went back to brooding over his coffee.
etymology: From Latin 'Saturnus'; in medieval astrology, those born under the slow, cold planet Saturn were thought to be sluggish and grave.

definition: Elegantly harmonious, with every part fitting neatly and gracefully together.
exampleSentence: The essay's concinnous structure made each argument slide effortlessly into the next.
etymology: From Latin 'concinnus' (skilfully put together, neat); harmony achieved through fine proportion.

definition: Given to wandering about at night.
exampleSentence: His noctivagant habits meant the city's empty 3 a.m. streets felt like home.
etymology: From Latin 'nox, noctis' (night) + 'vagari' (to wander); a night-wanderer.

definition: Spontaneously playful, done for the sheer fun of it.
exampleSentence: Her ludic doodles crept into the margins of every serious report.
etymology: From French 'ludique', from Latin 'ludus' (play, game); pertaining to undirected, joyful play.

definition: Mysteriously entrancing, as if possessing a hidden, oracular power.
exampleSentence: The cellist drew an orphic hush over the entire candlelit hall.
etymology: From Orpheus, the Greek musician whose song could charm beasts, stones and even the dead; hence mystically beautiful and spellbinding.

definition: Worn out, exhausted and feeling a bit under the weather.
exampleSentence: After the night shift she felt fair wabbit and crawled straight into bed.
etymology: Scots; an expressive word for being drained or run-down. In the Dictionaries of the Scots Language.

definition: In a secretive, muddled and disorderly fashion.
exampleSentence: The plans were drawn up hugger-mugger, and no two people agreed on them.
etymology: English, of uncertain sixteenth-century origin; long used by Shakespeare and others for furtive, confused concealment.

definition: At full gallop; headlong and at great speed.
exampleSentence: The children went tantivy down the hill the moment the gate swung open.
etymology: English, seventeenth-century, perhaps imitative of a galloping horse's hoofbeats; also a hunting cry.

definition: A weary sadness that settles in when the world as it is falls short of the world as you wish it were.
exampleSentence: Reading the headlines over breakfast left him sunk in a quiet weltschmerz for the rest of the day.
etymology: German, 'Welt' (world) + 'Schmerz' (pain); coined by the author Jean Paul (Johann Paul Friedrich Richter) in his 1827 novel 'Selina', per Merriam-Webster.

definition: The bind of being forced to act when every available move only worsens your position.
exampleSentence: Whichever colleague she promoted, someone would quit; she was caught in a corporate zugzwang.
etymology: German, 'Zug' (move) + 'Zwang' (compulsion); a chess term in Merriam-Webster, 'the necessity of moving in chess when it is to one's disadvantage', now used figuratively.

definition: A charming, impractical dreamer who seems to live on air, with no settled business or income.
exampleSentence: My uncle is a lovable luftmensch, forever sketching grand inventions he will never quite build.
etymology: Yiddish 'luftmentsh', from 'luft' (air) + 'mentsh' (person); Merriam-Webster cites Israel Zangwill's 1907 'Ghetto Comedies' as an early English use.

definition: Emphatically nothing at all; not the slightest amount.
exampleSentence: I worked all summer on that pitch and got bubkes for it — not even a thank-you.
etymology: Yiddish 'bobkes', probably shortened from 'kozebubkes' (literally 'goat droppings'), related to a Slavic word for beans; defined in Merriam-Webster as 'the least amount; nothing'.

definition: A restless soul who is forever off seeking the next bit of fun or company.
exampleSentence: Retirement turned my quiet neighbour into a gadabout, always away at some fair or festival.
etymology: English, from the verb phrase 'gad about' (to roam in search of pleasure) + the suffix '-about'; defined in Collins as 'a person who restlessly seeks amusement'.

definition: The dogged stamina to stay seated and grind patiently through long, demanding work.
exampleSentence: Finishing a doctorate is less about genius than sitzfleisch — the ability to keep your seat for years.
etymology: German/Yiddish, literally 'sitting-flesh'; the OED records it from an 1877 citation in the International Review, meaning the power to endure or persevere.

definition: A clever, frugal, improvised fix that solves a problem with whatever scant resources are at hand.
exampleSentence: With no charger in sight, he rigged a jugaad from two stray wires and somehow it worked.
etymology: Hindi 'jugāṛ' (a combination of means and materials), from Sanskrit; in the OED with earliest evidence from a 1995 Wall Street Journal article, and in Collins as 'a resourceful approach to problem-solving'.

definition: A misheard word or phrase swapped for a similar-sounding one that still makes its own odd sense.
exampleSentence: Writing 'for all intensive purposes' is a classic eggcorn that almost sounds right.
etymology: Itself an eggcorn ('egg corn' for 'acorn'); coined by linguist Geoffrey K. Pullum on the Language Log blog in September 2003 and added to the OED in 2010.

definition: An accidental swap of the opening sounds of two words, often with comic results.
exampleSentence: He meant 'a well-oiled bicycle' but produced the spoonerism 'a well-boiled icicle'.
etymology: Named after the Rev. William Archibald Spooner (1844–1930), Oxford don famed for such slips, though most attributed examples are apocryphal; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Severe social withdrawal in which a person seals themselves away from the world for months or years.
exampleSentence: After the breakdown he became a hikikomori, ordering food online and barely leaving his room.
etymology: Japanese, from 'hiku' (to pull back) + 'komoru' (to seclude oneself); popularised by psychiatrist Tamaki Saitō (1998) and listed in the OED.

definition: Someone who stays loftily aloof from party politics, perched on the fence between sides.
exampleSentence: He cast himself as a principled mugwump, refusing to back either candidate on offer.
etymology: From Massachusett (Algonquian) 'mugquomp' (war leader, important person); the political sense dates to the 1884 US election, per Merriam-Webster.

definition: To make bigger or more expansive.
exampleSentence: Tap the map twice to embiggen the street names until you can actually read them.
etymology: A mock-archaic coinage by writer Dan Greaney for The Simpsons episode 'Lisa the Iconoclast' (aired 18 Feb 1996), in the motto 'A noble spirit embiggens the smallest man'; added to Merriam-Webster in 2018.

definition: To snatch a property deal by raising the price after already agreeing a lower one with a buyer.
exampleSentence: They had shaken hands on the cottage, only to be gazumped by a cash offer the next morning.
etymology: British; an earlier sense 'to swindle' is attested from 1928, origin uncertain (often linked to Yiddish but listed as uncertain by the OED); the property sense dates from about 1971. In Collins.

definition: Acceptable, legitimate, and perfectly fine — said with a knowing wink.
exampleSentence: 'Irregardless' may grate, but plenty of speakers treat it as a wholly cromulent word.
etymology: Coined by writer David X. Cohen for The Simpsons episode 'Lisa the Iconoclast' (aired 18 Feb 1996), in the line 'It's a perfectly cromulent word'; added to the OED in 2018.

definition: Drily and slyly witty, with a quietly cunning humour.
exampleSentence: His pawky asides at the funeral somehow made everyone smile without breaking the solemnity.
etymology: Scots and Northern English, from 'pawk' (a trick or wile, of obscure origin); in Collins and the OED meaning shrewdly or drily humorous.

definition: Undeservedly lucky — landing good fortune without earning it.
exampleSentence: He revised nothing and still aced the exam, the jammy so-and-so.
etymology: British informal, from 'jam' (as slang for something easy or desirable) + '-y'; defined in Collins as lucky.

definition: Unusually sensitive to cold or discomfort; soft and easily chilled.
exampleSentence: Call me nesh, but I need three jumpers the moment the thermostat dips below twenty.
etymology: From Old English 'hnesce' (soft, tender, weak), surviving in Midland and Northern English dialect; in Collins and the OED.

definition: Excessively dainty, quaint, or cute to the point of being cloying.
exampleSentence: The café was almost too twee, all gingham bunting and hand-lettered jam-jar labels.
etymology: Early 20th-century British, a baby-talk alteration of 'sweet'; the OED's first citation is from Punch in 1905. In Collins and Merriam-Webster.

definition: Slow-witted and clueless, with a blank lack of sense.
exampleSentence: He gave a gormless shrug when asked where he'd parked the company van.
etymology: Alteration of dialectal 'gaumless', from 'gaum' (heed, understanding, from Old Norse 'gaumr') + '-less'; in Collins, Merriam-Webster, and the OED.

definition: Offensively pushy and full of one's own importance.
exampleSentence: The new intern was so bumptious he tried to redesign the whole department in week one.
etymology: Early 19th-century jocular blend of 'bump' with an ending modelled on 'fractious'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: So sentimental it tips over into sickly and insincere.
exampleSentence: The film's mawkish ending, all swelling strings and slow-motion tears, made the audience squirm.
etymology: From obsolete 'mawk' (maggot), from Old Norse 'mathkr', + '-ish'; originally 'nauseating', now 'sickly sentimental'. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Whether one likes it or not; or, in a haphazard, unplanned way.
exampleSentence: The reorganisation swept them all into new teams willy-nilly, with no say in the matter.
etymology: An alteration of 'will I, nill I' — from 'nill' (Old English 'nyllan', to be unwilling); attested from about 1608, in Merriam-Webster.

definition: By necessity; unavoidably and of necessity.
exampleSentence: With the bridge washed out, they perforce took the long road around the valley.
etymology: Middle English from Anglo-French 'par force' (by force); in Merriam-Webster, dating to the 14th century.

definition: A song or poem of lamentation for the dead.
exampleSentence: The composer wrote a quiet threnody for the victims of the flood.
etymology: From Greek 'threnoidia', from 'threnos' (lament) + 'oide' (song); in English from the 17th century and in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Something reused or altered but still bearing visible traces of its earlier form.
exampleSentence: The old city is a palimpsest, each era's streets written over the last.
etymology: From Greek 'palimpsestos' (scraped again), from 'palin' (again) + 'psen' (to scrape); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: A gap or missing portion, especially in a manuscript or an argument.
exampleSentence: There is a frustrating lacuna in the diary right where the scandal began.
etymology: From Latin 'lacuna' (pool, pit, gap), diminutive of 'lacus' (lake); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The bold treatment of light and shadow, especially in painting.
exampleSentence: Candlelight threw the room into a dramatic chiaroscuro of gold and black.
etymology: From Italian 'chiaro' (clear, light) + 'oscuro' (dark, obscure); in Merriam-Webster from the 17th century.

definition: A deliberate pause or break, as in a line of verse or a piece of music.
exampleSentence: She let a long caesura fall before delivering the verdict.
etymology: From Latin 'caesura' (a cutting), from 'caedere' (to cut); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: A person or thing that is the centre of attention or admiration.
exampleSentence: In her emerald gown she was the cynosure of the entire ballroom.
etymology: From Greek 'kynosoura' (dog's tail), the old name for Ursa Minor and the Pole Star; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Radiant, shining splendour.
exampleSentence: Dawn broke over the bay in a slow refulgence of rose and copper.
etymology: From Latin 'refulgere' (to shine back), from 're-' + 'fulgere' (to shine); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Land or a domain held and ruled directly by its owner.
exampleSentence: The old lord rarely left the wooded demesne his family had held for centuries.
etymology: From Anglo-French 'demesne', a variant of 'demeine' (belonging to a lord), from Latin 'dominicus'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A place where one habitually goes; one's usual haunts or surroundings.
exampleSentence: The narrow cafes of the old quarter were the poet's favourite purlieu.
etymology: From Anglo-French 'puralee' (a going over, a perambulation of boundaries); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: An interval during which normal authority or activity is suspended.
exampleSentence: In the interregnum between governments, no one was quite sure who was in charge.
etymology: From Latin 'inter' (between) + 'regnum' (reign, rule); in Merriam-Webster from the 16th century.

definition: A tedious, overlong passage in a book, film, or performance.
exampleSentence: The thriller was gripping despite a few longueurs in the middle act.
etymology: From French 'longueur' (length), from 'long'; borrowed into English in the 18th century and listed in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An awkward or unfortunate mishap, often a minor social clash.
exampleSentence: A small contretemps over the seating nearly ruined the rehearsal dinner.
etymology: From French 'contretemps' (against time, mistimed), from 'contre' + 'temps'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The highest or most glorified point of something; elevation to divine status.
exampleSentence: That final symphony is widely seen as the apotheosis of his career.
etymology: From Greek 'apotheosis', from 'apotheoun' (to deify), from 'theos' (god); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A region of partial shadow; figuratively, a shadowy borderland or grey area.
exampleSentence: The new rules left small businesses in a penumbra of uncertainty.
etymology: Coined in Latin by the astronomer Kepler from 'paene' (almost) + 'umbra' (shadow); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: A servant or assistant who handles many different kinds of work.
exampleSentence: As the firm's general factotum, she did everything from filing to fixing the boiler.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'fac totum' (do everything), from 'facere' (to do) + 'totum' (the whole); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rigid stickler for rules and discipline.
exampleSentence: The new manager was a martinet who timed our coffee breaks to the second.
etymology: Named after Jean Martinet, a 17th-century French army officer notorious for harsh drill; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The moment in a drama when a character makes a crucial discovery or recognition.
exampleSentence: The play's anagnorisis arrives when the king learns the beggar is his son.
etymology: From Greek 'anagnorisis' (recognition); a key term in Aristotle's 'Poetics' and a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: The strained or incorrect use of a word, sometimes for deliberate effect.
exampleSentence: Shakespeare's 'sea of troubles' is a celebrated catachresis of clashing images.
etymology: From Greek 'katachresis' (misuse), from 'katachresthai' (to misuse); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Fleeting; lasting only a very short time.
exampleSentence: Cherry blossom is loved partly for its fugacious, week-long beauty.
etymology: From Latin 'fugax' (apt to flee), from 'fugere' (to flee); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: So light and delicate as to be almost transparent.
exampleSentence: A diaphanous curtain stirred at the window in the warm evening air.
etymology: From Greek 'diaphanes' (showing through), from 'dia-' (through) + 'phainein' (to show); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Easily broken or fragile.
exampleSentence: Handle the antique vials gently; the old glass is dangerously frangible.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'frangibilis', from Latin 'frangere' (to break); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Elegant, precise, and polished, especially of language.
exampleSentence: His acceptance speech was short, lapidary, and quoted for years afterward.
etymology: From Latin 'lapidarius' (of stone), from 'lapis' (stone); the sense evokes words fit to carve in stone. In Merriam-Webster.

definition: Prophetic; like an inspired seer or oracle.
exampleSentence: The old poet spoke in a vatic murmur, as if reading some hidden future.
etymology: From Latin 'vates' (seer, prophet, poet); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Repellent, irritating, or off-putting.
exampleSentence: The report's rebarbative jargon scared off the very readers it needed.
etymology: From French 'rebarbatif', from 'se rebarber' (to face one another beard to beard); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Impossible to avoid or escape; inevitable.
exampleSentence: Ageing felt sudden, though it had been an ineluctable fact all along.
etymology: From Latin 'ineluctabilis', from 'in-' (not) + 'eluctari' (to struggle out); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Dizzyingly high, steep, or rapidly changing.
exampleSentence: From the vertiginous ledge the climbers looked like tiny ants below.
etymology: From Latin 'vertigo' (a whirling, dizziness), from 'vertere' (to turn); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Of or relating to the underworld; dark and earthbound.
exampleSentence: The myth describes a chthonic god who rules beneath the roots of the world.
etymology: From Greek 'chthon' (earth, ground); a Merriam-Webster headword used especially of underworld deities.

definition: Sharply caustic or biting, especially in wit.
exampleSentence: Her mordant reviews could end a play's run in a single paragraph.
etymology: From French 'mordant', present participle of 'mordre' (to bite), from Latin 'mordere'; in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Inclined to split into factions or break apart.
exampleSentence: The fissiparous party spent more energy fighting itself than its rivals.
etymology: From Latin 'fissus' (split), from 'findere' (to cleave), + '-parous' (producing); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To depict or describe something, especially in fine detail.
exampleSentence: The novel limns small-town life with tenderness and a sharp eye.
etymology: From Anglo-French 'luminer' (to illuminate a manuscript), from Latin 'luminare' (to light up); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To outline faintly or foreshadow something to come.
exampleSentence: Her early sketches adumbrate the bold style of her later murals.
etymology: From Latin 'adumbrare' (to cast a shadow, sketch), from 'ad-' + 'umbra' (shadow); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To study or write laboriously, especially late into the night.
exampleSentence: He lucubrated until dawn, surrounded by coffee cups and open books.
etymology: From Latin 'lucubrare' (to work by lamplight), from 'lux' (light); in Merriam-Webster and the OED.

definition: To protest or denounce loudly and vehemently.
exampleSentence: The columnist fulminated for pages against the new parking fines.
etymology: From Latin 'fulminare' (to strike with lightning), from 'fulmen' (thunderbolt); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To travel or wander from place to place.
exampleSentence: After graduating they peregrinated across the continent with one battered rucksack.
etymology: From Latin 'peregrinari' (to travel abroad), from 'peregrinus' (foreign); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: To win over or coax by flattery or cunning persuasion.
exampleSentence: She inveigled her way backstage with a confident smile and a fake badge.
etymology: From Anglo-French 'enveogler' (to blind, beguile), ultimately from Latin 'ab oculis' (without eyes); in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An ardent longing, especially grief for something cherished and now lost.
exampleSentence: A quiet desiderium for her grandmother's kitchen overtook her each autumn.
etymology: From Latin 'desiderium' (longing, grief for what is lost); a headword in Merriam-Webster and the OED, whose earliest English evidence is from 1715 in the writing of Jonathan Swift.

definition: A short, pointed, instructive saying that distils a truth.
exampleSentence: He answered every crisis with the same weary apothegm about haste and waste.
etymology: From Greek 'apophthegma' (something clearly spoken), via French; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, first used in English in 1548.

definition: Laborious, often nocturnal study, or the weighty writing it produces.
exampleSentence: His midnight lucubrations filled a dozen notebooks no one would ever read.
etymology: From Latin 'lucubrare' (to work by lamplight), akin to 'lux' (light); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, attested from the 1590s.

definition: Gentleness of manner; mildness, as of a creature made tame.
exampleSentence: She handled the frightened child with a mansuetude that calmed the whole room.
etymology: From Latin 'mansuetudo', from 'manus' (hand) + 'suescere' (to accustom), the idea of an animal grown used to the hand; a Merriam-Webster and Collins headword from the 14th century.

definition: An item of food, especially a choice or particularly tasty dish.
exampleSentence: The table groaned under viands no one at that lean table had seen in months.
etymology: From Old French 'viande' (food), from Latin 'vivenda' (things to live on), from 'vivere' (to live); a Merriam-Webster and Collins headword from the 14th century.

definition: Boastful, blustering talk; vainglorious bragging.
exampleSentence: His victory speech was pure rodomontade, all thunder and no actual plan.
etymology: From French 'rodomontade', after Rodomonte, the boastful Saracen king of Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso'; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword from the late 1500s.

definition: A person who writes from another's dictation or copies manuscripts; a literary assistant.
exampleSentence: Blind in old age, the poet dictated each canto to a patient amanuensis.
etymology: From Latin '(servus) a manu' (slave at hand, for writing) + '-ensis'; a Merriam-Webster, Collins and OED headword from the early 1600s.

definition: Radiant splendour; a brilliant shining-forth of light.
exampleSentence: The cathedral's east window flooded the nave with a gold effulgence at dawn.
etymology: From Late Latin 'effulgentia', from 'effulgere' (to shine forth), from 'ex-' (out) + 'fulgere' (to shine); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, used by Milton in 'Paradise Lost' (1667).

definition: The essence that makes a thing precisely what it is.
exampleSentence: In three brushstrokes he caught the very quiddity of a startled cat.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'quidditas', from Latin 'quid' (what); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword from the late 1500s.

definition: A fresh breaking-out of something after a period of dormancy.
exampleSentence: Spring brought a recrudescence of the old quarrel between the neighbouring farms.
etymology: From Latin 'recrudescere' (to become raw again), from 're-' + 'crudus' (raw); a Merriam-Webster headword from the 18th century.

definition: A person in ragged, tattered clothing.
exampleSentence: A cheerful tatterdemalion played a fiddle on the corner, hat upturned for coins.
etymology: A 17th-century English coinage from 'tatter', with a fanciful mock-Latin ending; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: A bundle or burden, especially a wearisome weight one must carry.
exampleSentence: He shouldered the fardel of the family debts without a word of complaint.
etymology: From Old French 'fardel' (little bundle); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, famously used in Hamlet's 'who would fardels bear' soliloquy.

definition: A harsh, overbearing, quarrelsome person, especially a domineering woman.
exampleSentence: The landlady was a termagant who terrorised every tenant over the rent.
etymology: From 'Tervagant', an imaginary deity portrayed as violent in medieval mystery plays; a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: The process of exact, methodical reasoning from premises to conclusion.
exampleSentence: The detective solved it by pure ratiocination, never once leaving his armchair.
etymology: From Latin 'ratiocinari' (to calculate, reason), from 'ratio' (reckoning); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: Excessive, uncontrollable, often incoherent talkativeness.
exampleSentence: His emails suffered from such logorrhea that the actual request hid on page three.
etymology: From Greek 'logos' (word) + 'rhoia' (flow); a Merriam-Webster headword (also spelled 'logorrhoea').

definition: Strongly abusive language, or the disgrace it brings on its target.
exampleSentence: The whistle-blower endured years of obloquy before being publicly vindicated.
etymology: From Late Latin 'obloquium' (speaking against), from 'ob-' + 'loqui' (to speak); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: Given to using long words; (of a word) ponderously many-syllabled.
exampleSentence: His sesquipedalian style buried a simple idea under three subordinate clauses.
etymology: From Latin 'sesquipedalis' (a foot and a half long), echoing Horace's 'sesquipedalia verba' in his 'Ars Poetica'; a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Misty and dark; dim with gloom.
exampleSentence: They groped down the caliginous stairwell, the single bulb long dead.
etymology: From Latin 'caliginosus' (misty), from 'caligo' (darkness, fog); a Merriam-Webster and Collins headword from 1548.

definition: Excessively or dotingly fond of one's wife.
exampleSentence: So uxorious was the duke that he cancelled wars to be home for her birthday.
etymology: From Latin 'uxorius', from 'uxor' (wife); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword.

definition: Everlasting; enduring without apparent end.
exampleSentence: The lighthouse kept its sempiternal vigil over a coast that had drowned a hundred ships.
etymology: From Late Latin 'sempiternalis', from Latin 'semper' (always) + 'aeternus' (eternal); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Possessing or showing deep wisdom and discernment.
exampleSentence: She gave a sapient nod, as though she had foreseen the whole disaster.
etymology: From Latin 'sapiens', present participle of 'sapere' (to be wise, to taste); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To melt away or dissolve, gradually losing form.
exampleSentence: His resolve seemed to deliquesce the moment she walked back into the room.
etymology: From Latin 'deliquescere' (to melt away), from 'de-' + 'liquescere' (to become liquid); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: To cloud over or obscure, as with a fog.
exampleSentence: Jargon only obnubilated a report that should have taken one clear page.
etymology: From Latin 'obnubilare' (to cover with clouds), from 'ob-' + 'nubes' (cloud); a Merriam-Webster headword.

definition: Perhaps; by chance.
exampleSentence: Peradventure the road is clear by morning, and we may yet reach the coast.
etymology: From Old French 'par aventure' (by chance); a Merriam-Webster and OED headword, now archaic or playful.

definition: An alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the sun, earth, and moon, in a roughly straight line.
exampleSentence: During the eclipse the children learned they were witnessing a rare syzygy of sun, moon, and earth.
etymology: From Late Latin 'syzygia', from Greek 'syzygos' ('yoked together'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The slender figure-eight curve traced by the sun's position in the sky when photographed at the same time of day across a whole year.
exampleSentence: He bolted his camera to the balcony and, photographing the noon sun weekly, slowly captured a perfect analemma.
etymology: From Latin 'analemma', from Greek 'analemma' ('support, pedestal'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A faint oval glow in the night sky directly opposite the sun, caused by sunlight scattered back from interplanetary dust.
exampleSentence: Far from any town, with the moon down, she could just make out the ghostly gegenschein overhead.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Gegenschein' ('counter-shine'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of a pale greyish-yellow, parchment, or fawn colour.
exampleSentence: The old letters had faded to an isabelline hue that made them look centuries older than they were.
etymology: From the proper name Isabella, with the OED noting the colour-sense predates the popular legend; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: A pale grey-green colour, named after a type of glazed Chinese pottery.
exampleSentence: She painted the nursery a soft celadon that seemed to hold the calm of early spring.
etymology: From French 'céladon', after a character in d'Urfé's pastoral romance 'L'Astrée'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A deep saffron-to-mustard yellow pigment made from gum resin.
exampleSentence: The autumn ginkgo turned a blazing gamboge that lit up the whole grey street.
etymology: From New Latin 'gambogium', from 'Camboja' (Cambodia), source of the resin; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The paragraph mark (¶) used in writing and typesetting.
exampleSentence: He clicked the little pilcrow icon to reveal all the hidden formatting in his document.
etymology: Alteration of Middle English 'pylcrafte', ultimately from Greek 'paragraphos'; a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary and Collins.

definition: A nonstandard punctuation mark combining a question mark and an exclamation point (‽).
exampleSentence: His incredulous text—"You did what‽"—called out for an interrobang.
etymology: Coined 1962 by Martin K. Speckter from 'interrogation' + 'bang' (printers' slang for the exclamation mark); a headword in the Oxford English Dictionary.

definition: The hash or pound symbol (#).
exampleSentence: Long before it was a hashtag, the telephone company politely called it the octothorpe.
etymology: A 20th-century American coinage of disputed origin, 'octo-' for its eight points; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tiny dot placed over a lowercase i or j.
exampleSentence: In her elegant handwriting even the tittle over each i was a perfect little circle.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'titulus' ('inscription, heading'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A slanting line (/) used to separate alternatives, mark line breaks, or denote fractions.
exampleSentence: The editor told her to replace the clumsy 'and/or' and its virgule with a clearer phrase.
etymology: From French 'virgule' ('comma'), from Latin 'virgula' ('little rod'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A symbol (÷ or †) used to mark division or, historically, to flag a doubtful or spurious passage in a text.
exampleSentence: The scribe set a small obelus beside the verse he suspected was a later forgery.
etymology: From Late Latin 'obelus', from Greek 'obelos' ('spit, pointed pillar'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: An angled quotation mark (« or ») used in French and several other languages.
exampleSentence: The French novel framed every line of dialogue in graceful guillemets rather than the curly marks she knew.
etymology: French diminutive of 'Guillaume' (William), said to honour 16th-century typecutter Guillaume Le Bé; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A sudden breaking-off of speech, as if the speaker were unwilling or unable to continue.
exampleSentence: "Why, if I ever catch him, I'll—" and his furious aposiopesis hung in the air more menacingly than any threat.
etymology: From Late Latin, from Greek 'aposiopesis' ('a becoming silent'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: The insertion of a word or words into the middle of another word, as in "abso-bloomin-lutely."
exampleSentence: "Un-frickin-believable" is a cheerful piece of everyday tmesis.
etymology: From Greek 'tmesis' ('a cutting'), from 'temnein' ('to cut'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Writing in which alternate lines run in opposite directions, like an ox ploughing a field.
exampleSentence: The ancient inscription was carved in boustrophedon, so he had to read one line left to right and the next right to left.
etymology: From Greek 'boustrophedon' ('turning like oxen in ploughing'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tendency to perceive a specific, meaningful image, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous pattern.
exampleSentence: It was just pareidolia, of course, but she couldn't stop seeing a startled face in the electrical socket.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Pareidolie', from Greek 'par-' + 'eidolon' ('image'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The tendency to perceive meaningful connections or patterns between unrelated things.
exampleSentence: His conviction that the lottery numbers spelled out a message was textbook apophenia.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Apophänie', coined by psychiatrist Klaus Conrad in 1958; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A painting technique of blending tones so softly that outlines seem to vanish like smoke.
exampleSentence: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile owes everything to Leonardo's mastery of sfumato.
etymology: From Italian 'sfumare' ('to evaporate, tone down'), related to 'fumo' ('smoke'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A painting or decorative work executed entirely in shades of grey.
exampleSentence: The chapel ceiling was a sombre grisaille that mimicked carved stone relief.
etymology: From French 'gris' ('grey'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A vivid literary description of a work of visual art.
exampleSentence: Keats's poem on the Grecian urn is the most famous ekphrasis in English.
etymology: From Greek 'ekphrasis' ('description'), from 'ekphrazein' ('to recount, describe'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A European decorative style imitating Chinese motifs and ornament.
exampleSentence: The drawing room was full of blue-and-white chinoiserie, from the wallpaper to the lacquered cabinets.
etymology: From French 'chinois' ('Chinese'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Paint laid on so thickly that it stands up in ridges from the surface.
exampleSentence: Van Gogh's stars are built from swirls of impasto you can almost feel with your fingertips.
etymology: From Italian 'impasto' ('a paste, dough'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Decoration made by scratching through a surface layer to reveal a different colour beneath.
exampleSentence: The potter finished the vase with delicate sgraffito, scoring leaves through the dark glaze to the pale clay.
etymology: From Italian 'sgraffito' ('scratched'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Metalwork shaped into relief by hammering from the reverse side.
exampleSentence: The silver bowl's rim was decorated with vines in fine repoussé.
etymology: From French 'repousser' ('to push back'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The grooved wooden plug that forms the mouthpiece of a recorder or whistle.
exampleSentence: A crack in the fipple meant the old recorder could no longer hold a clean note.
etymology: Of uncertain origin, recorded from the 17th c.; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Elaborate ornamentation of a vocal melody with runs, trills, and leaps.
exampleSentence: The soprano's dazzling coloratura in the final aria brought the house to its feet.
etymology: From Italian 'coloratura' ('colouring'), from Late Latin 'coloratus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A rotating cage in a mechanical watch that counteracts the errors gravity introduces into timekeeping.
exampleSentence: Through the sapphire dial you could watch the tiny tourbillon turning once a minute.
etymology: From French 'tourbillon' ('whirlwind'); a headword in Collins.

definition: The end of the day; evening.
exampleSentence: At eventide the fishermen drew their boats up the shingle and lit their lamps.
etymology: From Old English 'ǣfentīd'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The early morning; dawn, when the rooster first calls.
exampleSentence: They rose at cockcrow to reach the market before the heat set in.
etymology: From 'cock' + 'crow', attested in Middle English; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: The part of the day between dawn and noon; the morning.
exampleSentence: He spent the whole forenoon mending nets and was finished well before lunch.
etymology: From 'fore-' + 'noon'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A full continuous period of one night and one day; twenty-four hours.
exampleSentence: The fever broke after a single exhausting nychthemeron at the bedside.
etymology: From Greek 'nykt-' ('night') + 'hēmera' ('day'); a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A period of seven nights; a week.
exampleSentence: "I shall return within a sennight," the messenger promised, "or not at all."
etymology: Contraction of Old English 'seofon nihta' ('seven nights'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Of or relating to winter; wintry.
exampleSentence: A hiemal hush lay over the fields, broken only by the crunch of frost underfoot.
etymology: From Latin 'hiemalis', from 'hiems' ('winter'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Wintry; relating to the winter or the winter solstice.
exampleSentence: They huddled by the fire through the long brumal nights.
etymology: From Latin 'brumalis', from 'bruma' ('winter solstice'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Snowy; resembling or full of snow.
exampleSentence: By morning the garden wore a niveous coat that softened every edge.
etymology: From Latin 'niveus', from 'nix' ('snow'); a headword in Collins.

definition: Granular old snow that has partly compacted on its way to becoming glacial ice.
exampleSentence: Above the treeline their boots crunched into the dense, year-old firn.
etymology: Borrowed from German/Swiss dialect 'firn' ('of last year'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A thin film of clear ice coating rock or other surfaces.
exampleSentence: A treacherous verglas on the granite slab forced the climbers to turn back.
etymology: From French 'verglas', from 'verre' ('glass') + 'glas' ('ice'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: Feathery white ice crystals that form on surfaces when water vapour freezes.
exampleSentence: The hoarfrost edged every blade of grass with tiny crystalline spines.
etymology: From Middle English 'hor' ('grey, white with age') + 'frost'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A coating of opaque white ice formed when supercooled fog droplets freeze on contact with a surface.
exampleSentence: After the freezing fog, the pines on the ridge were thick with rime.
etymology: From Old English 'hrīm'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A bright halo of light around the shadow of one's own head, cast on dewy grass.
exampleSentence: As he walked across the wet lawn at dawn, a faint heiligenschein crowned his shadow's head.
etymology: Borrowed from German 'Heiligenschein' ('holy shine, halo'), used in this optical sense from 1834; a headword in Merriam-Webster and Collins.

definition: A luminous cloud or radiant halo surrounding a figure or object.
exampleSentence: The streetlamp gave her a soft nimbus of gold in the foggy dark.
etymology: From Latin 'nimbus' ('rain cloud, halo'); a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A radiant halo of light, especially one around the sun or moon seen through thin mist.
exampleSentence: A pale aureole ringed the winter moon, promising frost by morning.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'aureola' ('golden'), from Latin 'aureus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A milky, shifting play of soft colours like that of an opal.
exampleSentence: The dawn sky took on a faint opalescence, pink and green bleeding into the grey.
etymology: From 'opal', from Latin 'opalus'; a headword in Merriam-Webster.

definition: A tiny trace, spark, or particle of something.
exampleSentence: There was not a scintilla of evidence to support the rumour.
